110380.q: Why is a mixed forest usually more stable than a plantation of only spruce?
a: Many species make it more resistant to pests and storms
Spruces do not grow at all in mixed forests
A mixed forest needs no water
No insects live in a mixed forest
110380.e: In a pure spruce plantation, the bark beetle, for example, can spread quickly. In a mixed forest, only some of the trees are lost when there is damage.

110381.q: What is usually at the start of a food chain on land?
110381.e: Every food chain begins with a producer, on land usually a green plant. Then come plant eaters and then meat eaters.
110381.m: Food chains begin with a producer, on land usually a plant.

a: The habitat of a community of living things
All the animals of an area together
A cycle of substances in the soil
110382.e: A biotope is a habitat that can be marked off, with certain conditions such as soil, water, light and temperature. A certain community of living things lives in it.
110382.m: A biotope is a habitat with typical conditions.

110383.q: What does the Greek word “topos” in the term biotope mean?
110383.e: Biotope is made up of the Greek words “bios” for life and “topos” for place. So a biotope is a “place of life”.
110383.m: Biotope literally means place of life.

110384.q: Which of the following examples is a biotope?
110384.e: A pond is a habitat with certain conditions, such as still water and a muddy bottom. The brown hare is a living thing, not a habitat.
110384.m: A pond is a typical biotope.

110385.q: What is meant by a stepping-stone habitat?
a: A small habitat that links larger habitats
A paved path through the forest
A biotope made only of stones
110385.e: Stepping-stone habitats such as small ponds or bushes lie between larger habitats. Animals can use them as stopovers to get from one habitat to the next.
110385.m: Stepping-stone habitats help animals to move between habitats.

110386.q: What is the habitat along a river that is regularly flooded called?
110386.e: Floodplains are flooded during high water and then dry out again. This change creates gravel banks, ponds and softwood forests with many species.
110386.m: Floodplains are shaped by the change between floods and dry periods.

110387.q: Which habitats does the federal government list in an inventory as “biotopes of national importance”?
110387.e: The federal government keeps inventories of biotopes of national importance, for example raised bogs, fens, floodplains, amphibian spawning sites and dry meadows and pastures.
110387.m: Raised bogs are among the biotopes of national importance.

110388.q: At a pond, what is part of the biotope and not of the community of living things?
110388.e: The biotope includes the non-living conditions such as temperature, light and the ground. Frogs, water lilies and dragonfly larvae are living things and belong to the community.
110388.m: Non-living conditions belong to the biotope.

110389.q: Why are no fish put into a pond meant for amphibians?
a: Fish make the water dirty at once
Fish make the pond dry out
110389.e: Many fish eat frogspawn and tadpoles. In ponds without fish, frogs, toads and newts therefore have a much better chance.
110389.m: A pond for amphibians is best left without fish.

110390.q: Why is dead wood left in the forest on purpose?
a: It is a home for beetles, fungi and woodpeckers
It protects the forest from thunderstorms
It makes the soil acidic and infertile
It keeps deer away from the forest
110390.e: Countless insects, fungi and mosses live in dead wood. Woodpeckers look for food there and make holes that other animals use later.
110390.m: Dead wood is a valuable habitat in the forest.

110391.q: What is meant by a biocoenosis?
a: All the living things in a particular habitat
The non-living part of a habitat
110391.e: The biocoenosis is the community of all the plants, animals, fungi and microorganisms that live together in a biotope.
110391.m: The biocoenosis is the community of living things in a biotope.

a: All the plants, animals and fungi in a pond
The water and the mud of a pond
110392.e: The biocoenosis includes all the living things that live together in a habitat. Water, mud and temperature are non-living and belong to the biotope.
110392.m: The biocoenosis includes all the living things in a habitat.

110393.q: What belongs to the biocoenosis of a forest floor?
110393.e: The biocoenosis includes all living things, even tiny bacteria. Minerals, water and oxygen are non-living.
110393.m: Bacteria are part of the community of living things too.

110394.q: Which living things in a community break down dead plants and animals?
110394.e: Decomposers such as bacteria, fungi and earthworms break down dead living things. This releases minerals that plants can take up again.
110394.m: Decomposers close the cycle of substances in the community.

110395.q: What belongs to the plant part of a forest's community of living things?
110395.e: Mosses and ferns are plants. Roe deer, foxes, beetles and ants are animals, and stones and water are non-living.
110395.m: The community of living things includes plants and animals.

110396.q: What often happens when all the predators of a prey species disappear from a community?
a: The prey species multiplies a lot
The prey species dies out at once
110396.e: Without predators, an important brake is missing. The prey animals become more numerous and can, for example, eat far too many plants.
110396.m: Predators keep the numbers of their prey in check.

110397.q: Why is the beaver considered a keystone species in its community?
a: It dams streams and creates habitat for many species
It is the largest animal by the water
It lives in only one single valley
110397.e: With its dams, the beaver creates ponds, wetlands and dead wood. Amphibians, dragonflies, fish and birds benefit from this.
110397.m: The beaver shapes habitats for many other species.

110398.q: What kind of relationship is there between the fox and the field vole?
110398.e: The fox hunts and eats voles. It is the predator, and the vole is the prey.
110398.m: The fox and the vole have a predator and prey relationship.

110399.q: Which carnivorous plant belongs to the community of many raised bogs?
110399.e: In a raised bog poor in nutrients, the sundew catches small insects with sticky hairs on its leaves. This gives it extra nutrients.
110399.m: In the bog, the sundew adds insects to its diet.

110400.q: In biology, what is a population?
a: All the living things of one species that live in the same area at the same time
All the living things of different species in a forest
All the plants on Earth added together
110400.e: A population is made up of the individuals of the same species in a certain area, for example all the brown trout in a stream.
110400.m: A population is made up of living things of the same species in the same area.

110401.q: 300 roe deer live in a forest of 60 km². What is the population density?
110401.e: You divide the number of animals by the area: 300 ÷ 60 = 5. So there are 5 roe deer per square kilometre.
110401.m: For density, you divide the number by the area.

110402.q: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. How many bacteria are there after one hour?
110402.e: In one hour there are three divisions: 1 becomes 2, then 4, then 8. This is exponential growth.
110402.m: In exponential growth, the number keeps doubling.

110403.q: What shape is the growth curve of a population that is getting close to its carrying capacity?
110403.e: At first the population grows slowly, then quickly and finally more slowly again until it reaches the limit. This creates an S-curve, called logistic growth.
110403.m: Limited growth gives an S-shaped curve.

110404.q: What usually happens to the number of lynx when there are lots of snowshoe hares?
a: It rises because there is lots of food
110404.e: Lots of prey means lots of food for the predators, so their numbers increase. When they then eat many hares, the number of hares drops again, and later so does the number of lynx.
110404.m: The number of predators follows the number of prey.

110405.q: A population has 200 animals. In one year, 50 young animals are added and 30 animals die. How many animals are there afterwards?
110405.e: You work out 200 plus 50 minus 30, which makes 220. Animals moving in or out are not counted here.
110405.m: A population grows when more animals are added than die.

110406.q: Apart from birth and death, which two processes change the size of a population?
110406.e: Animals can move into an area or leave it. Together with births and deaths, these movements determine the size of a population.
110406.m: Migration changes the size of a population.

110407.q: What does the ecological niche of a species describe?
a: Its role and needs in the ecosystem
Only the cave it lives in
Only the colour of its fur
110407.e: The ecological niche includes, for example, food, the time when it is active, temperature needs and enemies. It describes how a species lives in the ecosystem, not a place.
110407.m: The ecological niche is the role of a species in the ecosystem.

110408.q: How is the ecological niche different from the habitat?
a: The niche is the way of life, the habitat is the place where it lives
The niche is bigger than a continent
110408.e: The habitat tells you where a species lives. The niche tells you how it lives there, meaning what it eats and what conditions it needs.
110408.m: The habitat is a species' address, the niche its job.

110409.q: How can the blue tit and the great tit live side by side in the same broadleaved forest?
a: They look for food in different parts of the trees
One of them only lives there in winter
They are always fighting each other
110409.e: The light blue tit often searches on thin twigs and in the treetop. The heavier great tit searches more often on thicker branches and on the ground.
110409.m: Different ways of finding food let similar species live side by side.

110410.q: What do the different beak shapes of Darwin's finches on the Galápagos Islands show?
a: The finches use different sources of food
The finches are all the same age
The finches live in different countries
110410.e: Thick beaks crack hard seeds, thin beaks catch insects. This way the species have taken up different niches.
110410.m: The beaks of Darwin's finches suit their food.

110411.q: Hummingbirds in America and sunbirds in Africa are not closely related. Why do they still look alike?
a: They have a similar way of life and food
They fly between the continents every year
They both live only in cold regions
110411.e: Both feed on nectar from flowers and fill a similar niche. That is why both have developed long, thin beaks.
110411.m: Similar niches often lead to a similar appearance.

110412.q: Why do swallows and bats hardly get in each other's way when hunting insects?
a: Swallows hunt by day, bats at night
110412.e: Both catch flying insects, but at different times of day. By being separated in time, they share the food source.
110412.m: The time of day can also separate niches.

110413.q: Why is the niche a species actually uses usually smaller than the one it could use?
a: Because the animals are too lazy
Because the sun is too weak
Because animals only live for one year
110413.e: Without other species, a species could use a larger range (fundamental niche). Competitors and enemies limit this range (realised niche).
110413.m: Other species shrink the niche that a species actually uses.

110414.q: Which niche does the woodpecker mainly fill in the forest?
a: It looks for insects in the wood of trees
It catches fish in the lake
110414.e: With its strong beak, the woodpecker hacks holes in bark and wood. With its long tongue, it pulls out insect larvae.
110414.m: The woodpecker gets its food out of wood.

110415.e: The prefix “a” means “not”, and “bios” means life. Abiotic factors are non-living environmental factors such as light, temperature or water.
110415.m: Abiotic factors are non-living influences of the environment.

110416.q: Which of the following is an abiotic factor?
a: The pH value of the soil
110416.e: The pH value shows how acidic or alkaline the soil is. It is a chemical property, not a living thing.
110416.m: The pH value of the soil is an abiotic factor.

110417.q: Which abiotic factor decreases sharply with increasing depth in a lake?
110417.e: Water absorbs sunlight. That is why water plants and algae can only carry out photosynthesis in the upper layers of water.
110417.m: It gets dark in the depths of a lake.

110418.q: Why do different plants often grow on the south-facing slope of an alpine valley than on the north-facing slope?
a: The south-facing slope gets more sun and is warmer
It never rains on the south-facing slope
The north-facing slope has no soil
There is no wind on the north-facing slope
110418.e: In the northern hemisphere, the sun is in the south at midday. South-facing slopes therefore get more sunshine and are warmer and drier.
110418.m: Sunny south-facing slopes are warmer than shady north-facing slopes.

110419.q: Which abiotic factor mainly determines where the tree line lies in the Alps?
110419.e: Above a certain height, the growing season is too short and too cool for trees to thrive. That is why there is a tree line.
110419.m: The cold sets a limit for the forest in the mountains.

110420.q: Why does very warm river water become dangerous for fish such as the grayling?
110420.e: Less oxygen can dissolve in warm water. That is why many graylings died in the Rhine near Schaffhausen in the hot summer of 2018.
110420.m: Cold water contains more oxygen than warm water.

110421.q: Why does the wood anemone flower so early in spring in a beech forest?
a: Before the trees come into leaf, lots of light reaches the ground
The ground is driest in spring
It is too cold in the forest in summer
There are no insects in spring
110421.e: As soon as the beeches have leaves, it gets dark on the forest floor. Early flowering plants therefore use the light in spring before the canopy closes.
110421.m: Early flowering plants use the light before the trees come into leaf.

110422.q: Which adaptation helps many cacti to live with a lack of water?
a: They store water in their thick tissue
They have especially large, thin leaves
They evaporate a lot of water
110422.e: Cacti store water in their fleshy stems. Their leaves have turned into spines, so they lose little water through evaporation.
110422.m: Cacti are adapted to dry habitats.

a: An influence that comes from living things
An influence of the length of the day
110423.e: Biotic factors come from other living things, for example predators, prey, competitors or germs.
110423.m: Biotic factors come from living things.

110424.q: Which of the following is a biotic factor for a roe deer?
110424.e: The lynx is a living thing and hunts roe deer. Snow, temperature and the steepness of the slope are non-living factors.

110425.q: What kind of relationship is there between two roebucks fighting over the same territory?
110425.e: Animals of the same species need the same food and the same space. That is why they compete with each other, for example over territories.
110425.m: Animals of the same species can be competitors too.

110426.q: Which biotic factor is especially important for a good cherry harvest?
110426.e: Bees and other insects carry pollen from flower to flower. Without pollination, hardly any fruit forms.
110426.m: Without pollinating insects there is less fruit.

110427.q: What was the situation of the wolf in Switzerland before it returned from Italy in the 1990s?
a: It lived only in the National Park
It had never been native to Switzerland
110427.e: The wolf was wiped out in Switzerland in the 19th century. Since the 1990s, animals have been moving in again. As a predator, it affects red deer, roe deer and chamois.
110427.m: The wolf has returned to Switzerland since the 1990s.

110428.q: What is the camouflage colouring of many prey animals for?
a: To keep them warm in winter
110428.e: Colouring that matches the surroundings makes animals hard for predators to see. One example is the mountain hare with its white winter coat.
110428.m: Camouflage protects prey animals from their enemies.

110429.q: What kind of organism causes ash dieback, which has been found in Switzerland too since about 2008?
110429.e: Ash dieback is caused by a fungus brought in from East Asia (Hymenoscyphus fraxineus). Because of it, many ash trees lose shoots and die.
110429.m: Germs and disease-causing organisms are biotic factors.

110430.q: What are non-native species called that spread a lot and push out native species?
110430.e: Alien species are species that have reached new areas through humans. Some spread a lot, for example Japanese knotweed.
110430.m: Invasive alien species can push out native species.

110431.q: In biology, what is meant by competition?
a: Working together for each other's benefit
110431.e: Competition happens when several living things want to use the same limited resources, for example food, light or space.
110431.m: Competition is the contest for scarce resources.

110432.q: What often happens when two animal species need exactly the same food and the same space?
a: Over time, one species pushes out the other
Both species suddenly need no food
110432.e: If two species need exactly the same resources, the stronger species wins in the long run. The other disappears from the area.
110432.m: The same needs often lead to one species being pushed out.

110433.q: Two species of paramecium live with the same food in a jar. What happens after a while?
110433.e: A researcher carried out this experiment in the 1930s. The stronger species won the contest for food, and the other died out.
110433.m: In the contest for food, one species can push out another.

110434.q: Why is competition within a species often especially strong?
a: Because animals of one species have the same needs
Because animals of one species never meet
110434.e: Individuals of the same species need the same food, the same hiding places and the same space. That is why the contest between them is especially great.
110434.m: Members of the same species are often the strongest competitors.

110435.q: What do trees in a dense forest mainly compete for?
110435.e: Plants need light for photosynthesis. That is why trees in a dense forest grow tall, so as not to be shaded.
110435.m: In the forest, light is a scarce resource.

110436.q: Why do many songbirds defend a territory?
a: To make sure there is enough food for themselves and their young
To give food to other birds
110436.e: Robins, for example, keep others of their kind away by singing and threatening. This secures an area with enough food.
110436.m: Territories reduce the contest for food.

110437.q: Which introduced species is pushing out the native red squirrel in Great Britain?
110437.e: The grey squirrel, brought in from North America, is better at finding food than the native red squirrel. It also spreads a virus that is dangerous for red squirrels.
110437.m: In Great Britain, the grey squirrel is pushing out the red squirrel.

110438.q: Different species of tit look for food in different parts of a tree. What does this do for them?
a: They compete less with each other
They find no food at all this way
They can sing better this way
They always stay alone this way
110438.e: Some search on thin twigs, others on the trunk or on the ground. This way they use the food differently and get in each other's way less.
110438.m: If you search differently, you have less competition.

110439.q: What advantage does a shrub get when birds eat its berries?
a: The birds protect it from frost
110439.e: The seeds pass undigested through the birds' gut and are dropped in other places. The bird gets food, and the shrub gets its seeds spread.
110439.m: Birds and berry bushes benefit from each other.

110440.q: Which partners live in the tissue of many reef corals and supply them with nutrients?
110440.e: The algae carry out photosynthesis and give sugar to the coral. The coral offers them protection and nutrients; if the water is too warm, corals expel the algae and bleach.
110440.m: Reef corals live in symbiosis with algae.

110441.q: How do root nodule bacteria help plants such as clover or peas?
a: They take nitrogen from the air
110441.e: The bacteria live in nodules on the roots and make nitrogen from the air usable for the plant. In return, the plant supplies them with sugar.
110441.m: Root nodule bacteria supply legumes with nitrogen.

110442.q: Which fish lives protected among the tentacles of sea anemones?
110442.e: A layer of slime protects the clownfish from the anemone's stinging poison. It finds shelter there and defends the anemone against predators.
110442.m: The clownfish and the sea anemone help each other.

110443.q: Who helps cows to digest the cellulose in grass?
110443.e: Cows cannot break down cellulose themselves. Bacteria and other microorganisms in the rumen do this and get food and a sheltered place to live in return.
110443.m: Without the creatures in its rumen, the cow could hardly digest grass.

110444.q: What do cleaner fish do for larger fish?
a: They remove parasites from their skin
They keep them warm in winter
110444.e: Cleaner fish eat parasites and dead skin from larger fish. The larger fish get cleaned, and the cleaners get food.
110444.m: Cleaner fish and their customers benefit from each other.

110445.q: What do ants get from the aphids they protect?
110445.e: Aphids give off a sugary liquid called honeydew. The ants collect it and in return protect the aphids from enemies such as ladybirds.
110445.m: Ants protect aphids and get honeydew in return.

a: One living thing uses another and harms it
Two living things help each other
Two species avoid each other completely
An animal hunts its prey and kills it at once
110446.e: A parasite lives on or in another living thing and feeds on it. The host is harmed, but usually not killed straight away.
110446.m: A parasite lives at the expense of its host.

110447.q: Which group does the tick belong to, which sucks blood on the outside of its host?
110447.e: “Ecto” means outside. Ectoparasites such as ticks, fleas or lice live on the surface of their host's body.
110447.m: Ticks are ectoparasites because they live on the outside of the host.

110448.q: Which parasite lives in the gut of its host and is therefore an endoparasite?
110448.e: The tapeworm lives in the gut and takes in nutrients from the digested food through the surface of its body. “Endo” means inside.
110448.m: Endoparasites such as the tapeworm live inside their host.

110449.q: Why is mistletoe called a hemiparasite (half parasite)?
a: It carries out photosynthesis but takes water and minerals from the tree
It only lives for half a year
It only grows on half trees
It only harms every second tree
110449.e: The green leaves of mistletoe make their own sugar. But it taps water and minerals from the tree with sucking roots.
110449.m: Mistletoe is a hemiparasite on trees.

110450.q: Which bird lays its eggs in other birds' nests and lets other birds raise its young?
110450.e: The cuckoo is a brood parasite. The cuckoo chick often pushes the host birds' eggs out of the nest and is fed by the host parents.
110450.m: The cuckoo lets other birds raise its young.

110451.q: Which disease can be passed on by a tick bite?
110451.e: Ticks can pass on bacteria that cause Lyme disease, and viruses that cause tick-borne encephalitis (TBE). That is why you should check yourself for ticks after being in the forest.
110451.m: Ticks can pass on germs that cause disease.

110452.q: Which parasite harms honeybee colonies all over the world?
110452.e: The varroa mite sucks on bees and their brood and passes on viruses. Beekeepers therefore have to treat their colonies regularly.
110452.m: The varroa mite is a dangerous parasite of the honeybee.

110453.q: What does the tolerance range of a species tell you?
a: In which range of an environmental factor it can survive
How friendly it is to other animals
110453.e: For every environmental factor, for example temperature, there is a range between a minimum and a maximum. The species can only survive within it.
110453.m: Outside its tolerance range, a species cannot survive.

110454.q: What is the range called in which a living thing thrives best?
110454.e: In the optimum, the conditions are ideal and the living thing grows and thrives best. Towards the edges it gets harder and harder.
110454.m: A living thing does best in the optimum.

110455.q: How does a living thing get on when an environmental factor is close to the limit of its tolerance range?
a: It only just survives and hardly grows
110455.e: Close to the limits of the tolerance range, survival is only just possible. Growth and reproduction are very restricted. This range is called the pessimum.
110455.m: At the edge of its tolerance range, a living thing only just survives.

110456.q: The brown trout needs cool water rich in oxygen. What is true of its tolerance range?
110456.e: The brown trout can only cope with small changes in temperature and oxygen. Species with a narrow tolerance range are called stenoecious.
110456.m: The brown trout has a narrow tolerance range.

110457.q: Which of these animals is considered euryoecious, meaning it can adapt to very different conditions?
110457.e: The red fox lives in forests, in the mountains, in fields and even in cities such as Zurich. It has a wide tolerance range.
110457.m: Euryoecious species such as the fox can cope almost anywhere.

110458.q: What does a dense patch of stinging nettles indicate?
110458.e: Stinging nettles grow especially well where there is a lot of nitrogen in the soil, for example near dung heaps. Such plants are called indicator plants.
110458.m: Stinging nettles show soils rich in nitrogen.

110459.q: What does Justus von Liebig's law of the minimum say?
110459.e: If a single nutrient is missing, a surplus of other nutrients does not help. The factor in shortest supply determines growth.
110459.m: The factor in shortest supply limits growth.

110460.q: What shape is a typical tolerance curve?
110460.e: In the middle is the optimum with the highest life activity. On both sides the curve falls to the minimum and the maximum.
110460.m: A tolerance curve is usually shaped like a bell.

110461.q: What is the habitat of a species?
a: The typical place where the species lives
The body size of the species
110461.e: The habitat is the place where a species is typically found and finds everything it needs to live.
110461.m: The habitat is where a species lives.

110462.q: Which habitat does the Alpine ibex prefer?
a: Steep rocky areas in the high mountains
Damp floodplain forests on the Central Plateau
Dense spruce forests in the valley
110462.e: The ibex is a skilful climber on the rocks above the tree line. There it finds grasses and is safe from enemies.
110462.m: The ibex lives on steep rock in the high mountains.

110463.q: What is considered one of the main causes of the decline of many animal and plant species?
110463.e: When bogs are drained, hedges are cleared or land is built on, many species lose their habitat.
110463.m: Without a suitable habitat, no species can survive.

110464.q: Which habitat does the beaver need?
a: Water with trees on the bank
110464.e: The beaver lives by streams, rivers and lakes. It eats the bark and twigs of trees on the bank, such as willows and poplars.
110464.m: The beaver lives by water with trees and bushes on the bank.

110465.q: Unlike the biotope, what does the term habitat refer to?
a: To a whole community of living things
110465.e: A biotope is the living space of a whole community. We speak of a habitat when we mean the place where a particular species lives.
110465.m: A habitat belongs to a particular species.

110466.q: What are wildlife bridges over motorways for?
a: They link habitats that are cut apart by roads
They are car parks for foresters
They keep noise away from houses
110466.e: Motorways cut habitats apart. On wildlife bridges covered in plants, deer, foxes and other animals can cross the road safely.
110466.m: Wildlife bridges link habitats that have been cut apart.

110467.q: Why are amphibian fences put up along some roads in spring?
a: Toads then migrate to the water where they spawn
Newts then move into the towns
Toads flee onto the road from birds
110467.e: Many amphibians spend the winter on land and migrate to their pond in spring. The fences guide them into buckets so that helpers can carry them safely across the road.
110467.m: Amphibians need a habitat on land and a body of water.

110468.q: Which habitat does the skylark need?
110468.e: The skylark nests on the ground in open farmland. Because such land is farmed more intensively, it has become rare in Switzerland.
110468.m: The skylark lives in open meadows and fields.

110563.q: Why do you breathe in briefly and strongly when sniffing?
a: So that more scent molecules reach the smelling area at the top
So that the nose warms up faster
So that the smell cells rest for a moment
So that less dust gets into the lungs
110563.e: Sniffing creates swirls of air that carry the air up to the roof of the nose. That way more scent molecules reach the olfactory lining.
110563.m: Sniffing brings more scent molecules to the olfactory lining.

110564.q: What must happen to scent molecules before the smell cells can recognise them?
a: They dissolve in the mucus of the olfactory lining
They are warmed in the lungs
They first mix with the blood
They are broken up by the teeth
110564.e: The olfactory lining is covered by a thin layer of mucus. The scent molecules dissolve in it and so reach the smell cells.
110564.m: Scent molecules must first dissolve in the nasal mucus.

110565.q: Roughly how big is the olfactory lining of a human?
a: A few square centimetres on each side of the nose
About the size of a newspaper page
110565.e: The human olfactory lining is only a few square centimetres in size. In many animals with a good sense of smell it is much bigger.
110565.m: Our olfactory lining is only a few square centimetres in size.

110566.q: Where do the smell cells send their signals?
110566.e: The smell cells are connected directly to the brain by nerve fibres. That is where the impression of a smell arises.
110566.m: Smell signals go straight to the brain.

110567.q: How do the flavours reach the olfactory lining when you chew?
a: From behind, via the throat into the nose
Through the Eustachian tube into the ear
Through the blood into the nose
Through the tear ducts of the eyes
110567.e: When you chew and swallow, aromas rise from the mouth through the throat up into the nose. This is called retronasal smelling.
110567.m: When eating, we also smell from behind through the throat.

110568.q: Where in the nose is the olfactory lining?
a: Right at the top in the roof of the nose
At the back of the throat
110568.e: The olfactory lining is only about the size of a stamp and lies right at the top of the nose. That is why you sniff to smell scents better.
110568.m: Smelling happens right at the top of the nose.

110569.q: What does the olfactory lining in the nose detect?
110569.e: The olfactory lining contains smell cells. They recognise scent molecules that get into the nose with the air.

110570.q: What type of cell are smell cells?
110570.e: Smell cells are specialised nerve cells. They pick up scent molecules and send their signal themselves along an extension towards the brain.
110570.m: Smell cells are nerve cells in the nose.

110571.q: What is special about smell cells compared with most other nerve cells?
a: They are constantly replaced by new ones
They are the biggest cells in the body
110571.e: Most nerve cells last a lifetime. Smell cells, on the other hand, die after a few weeks and are formed again from stem cells.
110571.m: Smell cells renew themselves again and again.

110572.q: How many different kinds of smell receptor do humans have?
110572.e: Humans have a few hundred different smell receptors. From their combinations, the brain can tell a huge number of smells apart.
110572.m: With hundreds of receptor types we can tell countless smells apart.

110573.q: Roughly how many smell cells does a human have?
110573.e: There are several million smell cells in the olfactory lining. A dog, however, has many more.
110573.m: We have millions of smell cells.

110574.q: What do scent molecules attach to in the nose?
110574.e: Scent molecules bind to smell receptors on the smell cells. The discovery of these receptors won the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2004.
110574.m: Scent molecules attach to smell receptors.

110575.q: Why do smells often bring back especially strong memories and feelings?
a: Smell signals go directly to the parts of the brain for feelings and memory
The nose is directly connected to the heart
Smells are stored in the stomach
Smell cells have their own memory
110575.e: Smell signals reach the limbic system very directly, and it is important for feelings and memories. That is why a scent can instantly remind you of the past.
110575.m: Scents are closely linked to feelings and memories.

110576.q: What do smell cells have at their end, which sticks out into the nasal mucus?
110576.e: At the end of each smell cell there are tiny hairs called cilia. On them are the receptors that scent molecules attach to.
110576.m: Smell hairs catch scent molecules in the mucus.

110577.q: How many kinds of smell receptor does a single smell cell usually have?
110577.e: Each smell cell is specialised in one type of receptor. The brain recognises a smell from the pattern of which cells are active at the same time.
110577.m: Each smell cell has only one kind of smell receptor.

110578.q: Which cranial nerve connects the smell cells with the brain?
110578.e: The extensions of the smell cells together form the olfactory nerve (nervus olfactorius). It is counted as the first of the twelve cranial nerves.
110578.m: The olfactory nerve is the first cranial nerve.

110579.q: Where are the taste papillae found in humans?
110579.e: The tongue is covered with many small bumps, the papillae. Many of them contain taste buds.
110579.m: Taste papillae are on the tongue.

110580.q: Why does the surface of the tongue feel rough?
a: Because of the many small papillae
110580.e: A great many tiny papillae stand close together on the tongue. They make the surface rough and help with touch.
110580.m: The many papillae make the tongue rough.

110581.q: Which list names the five basic tastes correctly?
110581.e: The tongue recognises five basic tastes. Spicy is not a taste but a pain signal, and warm or cold is a temperature signal.
110581.m: There are five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.

110582.q: What are the tiny structures in the papillae called that contain the taste cells?
110582.e: The taste buds sit in the papillae. Each contains several dozen sensory cells that come into contact with saliva through a small opening.
110582.m: Taste buds contain the sensory cells for taste.

110583.q: Why does food taste of less when you have a bad cold?
a: Because the nose helps with tasting
110583.e: We sense many flavours through the nose. If it is blocked, the tongue only notices the basic tastes.
110583.m: Without your nose, food tastes bland.

110584.q: Why can you taste normally again a few days after burning your tongue?
a: The taste cells are constantly renewed
You get used to the burning
110584.e: Taste cells only live for about two weeks. Then they are replaced by new ones, so your sense of taste recovers.

110585.q: What is the savoury basic taste called that you can taste in stock, cheese or ripe tomatoes?
110585.e: Umami is Japanese and means something like “delicious”. The taste was first studied in a Japanese seaweed broth.
110585.m: Umami is the savoury basic taste.

110586.q: Which basic taste is mainly caused by sodium ions?
110586.e: Table salt is made of sodium and chloride ions. The sodium ions are recognised by certain taste cells.

110587.q: What has to happen to a flavour substance so that the tongue can taste it?
110587.e: Taste cells only recognise substances that are dissolved in saliva. That is why a completely dry tongue tastes almost nothing.
110587.m: You can only taste dissolved substances.

110588.q: In which fruits does capsaicin occur naturally?
110588.e: Capsaicin is the substance that makes chilli peppers hot. The more capsaicin a variety contains, the hotter it is.

110589.q: Which self-defence product often contains capsaicin from chillies as its active ingredient?
110589.e: Pepper spray contains an extract from chilli peppers with a lot of capsaicin. It irritates the eyes, nose and skin so strongly that an attacker can be fended off.
110589.m: Pepper spray works with the hot substance from chillies.

110590.q: Which scale is used to give the heat of chillies?
110590.e: The Scoville scale measures the amount of hot substances in chillies. Bell peppers have a value of 0; very hot varieties have values in the millions.
110590.m: The heat of chillies is measured in Scoville units.

110591.q: Why does milk ease the burning of chilli better than water?
a: Because capsaicin dissolves in fat but hardly in water
Because milk is always colder than water
Because water makes capsaicin chemically stronger
110591.e: Capsaicin is fat-soluble. Fat and certain proteins in milk take it up and wash it away, while water only spreads it around.
110591.m: Milk helps against chilli burn better than water.

110592.q: Which animals hardly feel the heat of capsaicin and so spread chilli seeds?
110592.e: The capsaicin receptor of birds hardly reacts to the substance. They eat the fruits and pass the seeds out again undamaged.
110592.m: Birds eat hot chillies without feeling the burn.

110593.q: What is capsaicin used for in medicine?
a: In plasters and creams against pain
As a sleeping pill for the night
110593.e: Capsaicin first irritates the pain fibres and, with longer use, makes them less sensitive. That is why it is found in heat plasters and pain-relief creams.
110593.m: Capsaicin in plasters can relieve pain.

110594.q: Why does chilli feel hot in your mouth even though it is not warm at all?
a: Capsaicin triggers the same sensors that also react to heat
Chilli rubs against the tongue and makes heat
110594.e: Capsaicin opens a receptor that normally responds to strong heat. That is why the brain reads the signal as burning.
110594.m: Chilli tricks the brain into sensing heat.

110595.q: Which part of a chilli pepper contains the most capsaicin?
110595.e: The pale dividing walls that the seeds hang from contain the most capsaicin. The seeds themselves only become hot because they stick to them.
110595.m: The heat is mainly in the pale inner walls of the chilli.

110596.q: Which two kinds of thermoreceptors does the skin have?
110596.e: The skin has separate sensory cells for cold and for warmth. Together they give us our sense of temperature.
110596.m: The skin senses cold and warmth with different receptors.

110597.q: Which thermoreceptors are more common in the skin?
110597.e: The skin has far more cold spots than warm spots. That is why cooling is noticed especially quickly.
110597.m: The skin has more cold receptors than warmth receptors.

110598.q: Why does a peppermint sweet feel cool in your mouth?
a: The sweet cools the mouth by several degrees
110598.e: Menthol activates a cold receptor without it really getting colder. The brain then reports “cool”.
110598.m: Menthol tricks you into feeling cold.

110599.q: You hold one hand in cold water and the other in warm water, then both in lukewarm water. What do you feel?
a: The hand that was cold feels warm, the other feels cool
Both hands feel exactly the same
Both hands feel nothing at all
Both hands feel it is hot
110599.e: The thermoreceptors mainly report the change compared with before. For the cold hand, lukewarm is warmer; for the warm hand, it is cooler.
110599.m: Our sense of temperature always compares with what came before.

110600.q: Where in the body are the temperature-sensitive nerve cells that monitor the temperature of the blood?
a: In the hypothalamus of the brain
110600.e: The hypothalamus is the body's temperature centre. It measures the blood temperature and triggers sweating or shivering when needed.
110600.m: The hypothalamus controls our body temperature.

110601.q: What is the sense called with which we feel warmth and cold through the skin?
110601.e: We sense warmth and cold with the thermoreceptors in the skin. This is called the sense of temperature.
110601.m: We feel warmth and cold with our sense of temperature.

110602.q: What do you feel when very hot water above about 45 °C touches your skin?
110602.e: From about this temperature, pain sensors also react. The burning warns you of a scald.
110602.m: Too much heat is felt as pain.

110603.q: What do you notice if you touch the skin point by point with a cold metal tip?
a: You only feel cold at certain points
You feel exactly the same cold everywhere
You only feel cold at the hairs
110603.e: The thermoreceptors are not everywhere but at individual cold and warm spots. In between, the skin only reports touch.
110603.m: We feel cold at individual cold spots on the skin.

110604.q: Which sensory cells do pit vipers use to sense the body heat of their prey, even in the dark?
110604.e: Pit vipers have pit organs between the eye and the nostril. These sense heat radiation so precisely that the snake can locate warm prey.
110604.m: Pit vipers sense warm prey with their pit organs.

110605.q: What do nociceptors report to the brain?
110605.e: Nociceptors are pain sensors. The word comes from the Latin “nocere”, meaning to harm.
110605.m: Nociceptors are the body's pain sensors.

110606.q: Which organ has no pain receptors itself?
110606.e: The brain processes pain, but its tissue itself has no pain receptors. A headache arises, for example, in the membranes around the brain and in blood vessels.
110606.m: The brain itself feels no pain.

a: Pain in a part of the body that is no longer there
Pain that only happens in dreams
Pain from light that is too bright
110607.e: After an amputation, people can feel pain in the missing arm or leg. It is thought that mainly the nervous system and the brain create this feeling.
110607.m: Phantom pain arises in the nervous system, not in the missing body part.

110608.q: Which stimuli do nociceptors react to?
a: Strong heat, strong pressure and harmful substances
110608.e: Nociceptors report anything that can damage tissue. This includes extreme temperatures, crushing and irritating chemicals.
110608.m: Nociceptors react to many kinds of dangerous stimuli.

110609.q: Which substances made by the body can dampen pain, for example during great effort?
110609.e: Endorphins work in a similar way to strong painkillers. The body releases them, for example, during stress or long endurance sport.
110609.m: Endorphins are the body's own painkillers.

110610.q: Why is it dangerous if a person cannot feel pain from birth?
a: They often do not notice injuries in time
They can no longer see properly
110610.e: Without pain, the warning signal is missing. People affected injure themselves more often, for example their bones or joints, without noticing.
110610.m: People who feel no pain easily miss injuries.

110611.q: After a knock, you often first feel a sharp, stabbing pain and then a dull pain. Why?
a: The signals travel along nerve fibres of different speeds
The blood slows down part of the pain
110611.e: Thin fibres with a myelin coating carry the first, stabbing pain quickly. Even thinner fibres with no coating at all are slower and deliver the dull pain.
110611.m: Fast and slow pain use different nerve fibres.

110612.q: Why does it often help to rub a spot you have knocked?
a: Touch signals can dampen the passing on of pain in the spinal cord
Rubbing cools the spot a lot
Rubbing makes the skin permanently numb
110612.e: In the spinal cord, touch signals can block the passing on of pain signals. That is why rubbing feels soothing.
110612.m: Rubbing can weaken pain signals in the spinal cord.

110613.q: What does a sensory receptor do with a stimulus?
a: It turns it into an electrical nerve signal
It passes it into the blood
110613.e: Sensory receptors translate light, pressure, scents or temperature into electrical signals. This is the only language the nervous system understands.
110613.m: Receptors translate stimuli into nerve signals.

110614.q: Which stimulus do the receptors in the skin that sense cold and warmth react to?
110614.e: Each type of receptor is specialised in one kind of stimulus. Warmth and cold receptors in the skin react to temperature.
110614.m: Each receptor reacts to a particular kind of stimulus.

110615.q: Which group do the sensory cells for smell and taste belong to?
110615.e: Smell and taste cells react to chemical substances. That is why they are counted as chemoreceptors.
110615.m: Smell and taste are chemical senses.

110616.q: Which receptors does the eye use to take in light?
110616.e: In the retina there are light-sensing cells, the rods and cones. They are called photoreceptors, from the Greek “phos” for light.
110616.m: Photoreceptors in the eye react to light.

110617.q: Why do you stop feeling your socks after a while?
a: The receptors get used to the unchanging stimulus
Blood stops flowing into your feet
110617.e: Many receptors report an unchanging stimulus more and more weakly over time. This getting used to it is called adaptation.
110617.m: After a while we hardly notice unchanging stimuli.

110618.q: Why do you see spots of light when you press firmly on your closed eyes?
a: The pressure stimulates the retina, and the brain reads this as light
More light gets through the eyelids
The blood in the eye starts to glow
110618.e: Even the wrong kind of stimulus, such as pressure, can excite the retina. The brain only knows light signals from there, so it reports spots of light.
110618.m: The brain always reads signals from the eye as light.

110619.q: Where does the actual perception of a stimulus, such as a smell, take place?
110619.e: The receptor only delivers a signal. Only the brain processes it and turns it into a smell, a picture or a feeling.
110619.m: A stimulus is only perceived in the brain.

110620.q: What can sharks sense with special sense organs on their heads?
a: Weak electric fields from prey animals
110620.e: Sharks have many small pores with electroreceptors on their heads. With these they can even find prey hidden in the sand.

110621.q: What is meant by the stimulus threshold?
a: The smallest stimulus strength that can just be noticed
The greatest stimulus strength you can bear
The place where a nerve ends
110621.e: A stimulus must reach a certain minimum strength to be noticed. This limit is the stimulus threshold.
110621.m: We only notice a stimulus above the stimulus threshold.

110622.q: What is a stimulus called that is too weak to be noticed?
110622.e: If a stimulus is below the threshold, it goes unnoticed. It is called subliminal.
110622.m: We do not notice subliminal stimuli.

110623.q: How does the hearing threshold for high sounds usually change with age?
a: It rises, so high sounds are heard less well
It falls, so you hear better
It stays the same all your life
It disappears by the age of 20
110623.e: With age, sensory cells in the inner ear are lost, especially those for high sounds. These sounds then have to be louder to be heard.
110623.m: In old age, high sounds need to be louder for you to hear them.

110624.q: Why does sunburn hurt even when touched lightly?
a: The pain threshold of the inflamed skin has dropped
The skin suddenly has more bones
The sun has removed the nerves
110624.e: Inflamed skin releases substances that make the pain sensors more sensitive. That is why even a T-shirt is enough to cause pain.
110624.m: With inflammation, the pain threshold drops.

110625.q: You only notice a change in weight when about 2 percent is added. How much must be added to 1,000 g?
110625.e: 2 percent of 1,000 g is 20 g. The heavier something is, the more has to be added for you to feel the difference.
110625.m: The stronger a stimulus is, the bigger a change has to be for us to notice it.

110626.q: What happens to the eye's stimulus threshold when you are in the dark for a long time?
a: It falls, so you see fainter light
It rises, so you see worse
It always stays exactly the same
110626.e: In the dark the eye adapts and becomes more and more sensitive. After a while you can make out things you could not see at first.
110626.m: In the dark, the eye becomes more sensitive over time.

110627.q: What does a nerve cell do when a stimulus goes over its threshold?
a: It always sends out a signal at full strength
It sends a signal half as strong
110627.e: A nerve signal is either triggered completely or not at all. This is called the all-or-nothing principle.
110627.m: Nerve cells fire according to the all-or-nothing principle.

110628.q: What does the difference threshold describe?
a: The smallest difference between two stimuli that you can still notice
The difference between day and night
The distance between two nerve cells
The time until a stimulus is forgotten
110628.e: You compare two stimuli, such as two sounds or two weights. The smallest difference you can just recognise is the difference threshold.
110628.m: The difference threshold shows how finely we can compare stimuli.

110629.q: Which kind of stimuli do mechanoreceptors react to?
110629.e: Mechanoreceptors are stimulated by being deformed. They are found in the skin, muscles, ear and blood vessels.
110629.m: Mechanoreceptors sense pressure, touch and stretching.

110630.q: Where does the skin have especially many touch cells?
110630.e: In the fingertips and lips the touch cells are packed very closely. That is why we feel the tiniest differences there, for example when reading Braille.
110630.m: Fingertips and lips are especially sensitive to touch.

110631.q: Why do you hardly feel your clothes on your skin after a short time?
a: The touch cells get used to the unchanging stimulus
The clothes make the skin numb
The clothes get lighter over time
The brain falls asleep in those places
110631.e: Many touch cells mainly report changes. If a stimulus stays the same, they hardly send any signals and we no longer notice it.
110631.m: Touch cells get used to unchanging stimuli.

110632.q: Which sensory cells in the inner ear are mechanoreceptors?
110632.e: In the inner ear, sound waves move tiny hairs on the hair cells. This movement is turned into nerve signals.
110632.m: We hear with mechanoreceptors in the inner ear.

110633.q: With your eyes closed, which sense lets you recognise a coin in your trouser pocket?
110633.e: Touch cells in the fingers feel pressure, shape and surface. That way you recognise the round, flat coin without looking.
110633.m: With the sense of touch you can recognise shapes without looking.

110634.q: What does a mechanoreceptor do when it is pressed?
a: It produces a signal for the nervous system
110634.e: Mechanoreceptors turn pressure or stretching into electrical signals. Nerves carry them to the brain, which turns them into a feeling such as touch.
110634.m: Mechanoreceptors turn pressure into nerve signals.

110635.q: Which animals use long whiskers to sense even the slightest movements of air?
110635.e: Whiskers, or vibrissae, sit in hair follicles with many mechanoreceptors. Cats use them to find their way even in the dark.

110636.q: Why can you feel a mosquito on your arm even if it hardly touches your skin?
a: Sensory cells at the hair roots report every movement of the tiny hairs
The mosquito gives off heat that you feel
Your eyes tell your skin about the mosquito
The mosquito gives an electric shock
110636.e: Around the hair roots there are nerve endings that notice even the tiniest movement of a hair. The hairs work like feelers.
110636.m: Body hairs work like delicate feelers.

110637.q: Which sense organ do fish use to feel water movements and currents?
110637.e: The lateral line runs lengthways along the fish's body. Its mechanoreceptors sense pressure waves from obstacles, enemies and prey.
110637.m: Fish sense water movements with their lateral line.

a: Sensing the position and movement of your own body
110638.e: Thanks to proprioception, you know where your own arms and legs are. This works even without looking.
110638.m: Proprioception is the sense of your own body.

110639.q: Where are the sensors that tell the brain how much a muscle is stretched?
110639.e: Tiny sensors lie in the muscle. When the muscle is stretched, they send signals to the spinal cord and brain.
110639.m: Muscles report for themselves how much they are stretched.

110640.q: For which activity is body awareness (proprioception) especially important?
110640.e: When balancing, the body constantly needs to know how the feet, legs and trunk are positioned. Proprioception provides these messages.
110640.m: You need good body awareness to balance.

110641.q: Which simple test does a doctor use to check proprioception?
a: Bringing your index finger to your nose with your eyes closed
Reading out letters on a board
Counting the pulse at the wrist
110641.e: Without your eyes you have to rely completely on your body awareness. If you hit your nose, proprioception is working well.
110641.m: With your eyes closed, you can see how good your body awareness is.

110642.q: What does body awareness (proprioception) tell the brain?
a: How the joints are positioned and how hard the muscles are pulling
110642.e: Sensors in muscles, tendons and joints report position, movement and force. That way the brain knows what the body is doing.
110642.m: Body awareness reports position, movement and force.

110643.q: After a ligament injury in the foot, which kind of training often improves proprioception?
a: Lying in bed for a long time
110643.e: On a wobble board or cushion, muscles and sensory cells constantly have to adjust. That way the foot learns again to notice wrong positions quickly.

110644.q: Why can you climb stairs in the dark without seeing your feet?
a: Because body awareness reports the position of your legs
Because your ears hear the steps
Because your skin glows in the dark
Because your eyes see more sharply in the dark
110644.e: Muscles, tendons and joints constantly tell the brain where the legs are. That is why you can find the steps without looking.
110644.m: Body awareness works even without your eyes.

110645.q: Why do you trip easily when a leg has “gone to sleep”?
a: Because the feedback about the position of the leg is missing
Because the muscle is permanently paralysed
Because the leg suddenly gets shorter
Because the bones have gone soft
110645.e: When a nerve has been pressed, hardly any signals come from the leg for a while. The brain does not know exactly where the foot is.
110645.m: Without body awareness in the leg, walking becomes unsteady.

a: A linking of sense impressions, such as seeing colours when hearing
An inflammation of the sense organs
The loss of the sense of taste
110646.e: With synaesthesia, a stimulus also triggers an impression in another sense. Some people, for example, see colours when they hear music.
110646.m: In synaesthesia, sense impressions are linked together.

110647.q: What is the form of synaesthesia called in which letters or numbers appear coloured?
110647.e: A grapheme is a written character. People with it might always see the A as red or the 7 as green.
110647.m: Some people see letters and numbers in colours.

110648.q: Roughly how many people have some form of synaesthesia?
a: Fewer than ten in the world
110648.e: Studies estimate that a few percent of people have synaesthetic perceptions. Many do not even know that it is anything special.
110648.m: Synaesthesia is rare, but not extremely rare.

a: As a special way of perceiving, not an illness
As a result of lack of sleep
As a vision problem that must be treated
110649.e: Synaesthesia usually does no harm and needs no treatment. Many people who have it find it enriching.

110650.q: Roughly what does the Greek word “synaesthesia” mean?
110650.e: It is made up of “syn” for together and “aisthesis” for sensation. It means several senses sensing together.

110651.q: How do a synaesthete's colour links behave over many years?
a: They always disappear at the age of ten
110651.e: Anyone who sees the 5 as blue, for example, still sees it as blue years later. Researchers use this consistency as a test for real synaesthesia.

110652.q: Which painter is often linked with synaesthesia because he translated music into colours and shapes?
110652.e: Kandinsky described experiencing sounds as colours. Many of his abstract paintings have musical titles such as “Composition”.

110653.q: What is often observed about synaesthesia in families?
a: It is more common in some families
It only comes from music lessons
110653.e: In some families, synaesthesia occurs in several members. That is why it is thought that genes play a part.
110653.m: Synaesthesia often runs in the family.

a: Loss of the sense of smell
Loss of the sense of touch
110654.e: Anosmia means that someone can no longer smell anything. The “an” means “without” in Greek.
110654.m: With anosmia you can no longer smell.

110655.q: With a blocked nose, what else do you often notice less well?
110655.e: A large part of what we feel as taste actually comes through the nose. If it is blocked, food tastes bland.
110655.m: Without a sense of smell, food tastes bland.

110656.q: Where in the nose are the smell cells?
a: Right at the top of the nasal cavity
110656.e: The olfactory lining is in the upper part of the nasal cavity. That is why you sniff to smell a scent better: more air gets up there.
110656.m: The smell cells are at the top of the nasal cavity.

110657.q: Which disease caused many people to suddenly lose their sense of smell from 2020 onwards?
110657.e: A sudden loss of smell was a typical sign of COVID-19. For most people affected, the sense of smell came back after weeks or months.
110657.m: COVID-19 could suddenly switch off the sense of smell.

110658.q: What danger do people with anosmia face in everyday life?
a: They cannot smell smoke, gas or food that has gone off
110658.e: The sense of smell warns of fire, gas leaks and spoilt food. Smoke alarms and use-by dates help people affected.
110658.m: Without a sense of smell, important warning signals are missing.

110659.q: How can you train your sense of smell again after losing it?
a: Sniff different scents carefully every day
Eat food that is as spicy as possible
110659.e: In smell training, you carefully sniff a few strong scents every day for weeks. This can help to strengthen the sense of smell.
110659.m: Regular smell training can strengthen the sense of smell.

110660.q: Apart from infections, what else can lead to anosmia?
110660.e: With a blow to the head, the delicate smell fibres at the skull bone can tear. Then no more smell signals reach the brain.
110660.m: Head injuries can also destroy the sense of smell.

110661.q: How does the sense of smell change in most people in old age?
a: It always stays exactly the same
It disappears by the age of 40
110661.e: With increasing age, many people's ability to smell declines. That is why older people often use more salt and seasoning.
110661.m: In old age, the sense of smell often gets weaker.

110756.q: What is a “keystone species” in an ecosystem?
a: A species on which many others depend
The largest species in the area
The rarest species in the area
110756.e: A keystone species strongly shapes its habitat. The beaver, for example, dams streams and so creates habitat for many other species.
110756.m: Many other species depend on a keystone species.

110757.q: What do the two parts of the word “biodiversity” mean?
110757.e: “Bio” comes from the Greek word for life, “diversity” from the Latin word for variety. The term was made famous by the biologist Edward O. Wilson.
110757.m: Biodiversity means the variety of life.

110758.q: Which international treaty to protect biological diversity was signed at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro?
110758.e: The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) was opened for signature at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. Switzerland is also a party to it.
110758.m: The 1992 Convention on Biological Diversity protects biological diversity worldwide.

110759.q: Which goal was set in 2022 in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework?
a: To protect 30 percent of the area
110759.e: By 2030, at least 30 percent of the Earth's land and sea areas are to be effectively protected. This goal is also called “30 by 30”.
110759.m: By 2030, 30 percent of the Earth's surface is to be protected.

a: The benefits of nature for people
110760.e: Ecosystem services are things nature does that we benefit from, such as pollination, clean drinking water or fertile soil.
110760.m: Nature provides services for us such as pollination and clean water.

110761.q: What is the International Day for Biological Diversity for?
a: To draw attention to protecting the variety of species
110761.e: The UN declared 22 May the Day for Biological Diversity. On this day, people should think about protecting animals, plants and habitats.
110761.m: 22 May is the Day for Biological Diversity.

110762.q: Which federal office in Switzerland is mainly responsible for protecting biodiversity?
110762.e: The Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN) is responsible for protecting nature and the landscape. For example, it publishes Switzerland's Red Lists.
110762.m: The FOEN looks after biodiversity in Switzerland.

110763.q: What are areas of the Earth called that have especially many species and are also under great threat?
110763.e: Biodiversity hotspots are regions with very many species, often found nowhere else, whose original habitats have already shrunk a lot. Examples are Madagascar or the Mediterranean region.
110763.m: Hotspots are areas rich in species and also under threat.

110764.q: Which habitat on land is considered the richest in species on Earth?
110764.e: In tropical rainforests, especially many species live in a small area. The reasons are warmth, moisture and a stable climate.
110764.m: The tropical rainforest is the habitat on land with the most species.

110765.q: Which group of animals has the most known species?
110765.e: More than half of all described animal species are insects. Beetles alone have several hundred thousand species.
110765.m: Insects are the group of animals with the most species.

110766.q: Roughly how does the variety of species change as you go from the poles towards the equator?
110766.e: Towards the equator, the number of species usually rises clearly. Warmth and lots of solar energy favour great variety.
110766.m: The variety of species increases towards the equator.

110767.q: Roughly how many species have been scientifically described worldwide?
110767.e: So far, around two million species have been described. Experts think there are many more species still undiscovered.
110767.m: Around two million species have been described, and many more are still unknown.

110768.q: Which sea habitat is considered especially rich in species and is often called the “rainforest of the sea”?
110768.e: Coral reefs cover only a tiny part of the sea floor, but they are home to a large share of all sea species.
110768.m: Coral reefs are the rainforests of the sea.

110769.q: Which meadows are among the habitats richest in species in Switzerland?
110769.e: Poor, dry meadows are not fertilised. Many different flowers grow there, which in turn give food to many insects.
110769.m: Poor dry meadows are especially rich in species.

110770.q: What is a species called that has been brought to a new area by humans and pushes out native species there?
110770.e: Invasive species spread a lot and threaten native species. In Switzerland, for example, Himalayan balsam is an invasive alien plant.
110770.m: Invasive species push out native species.

110771.q: What is the name of an invasive plant from North America that often grows on railway embankments in Switzerland and has golden-yellow flowers?
110771.e: Canadian goldenrod forms dense patches and pushes out native plants. In Switzerland it is considered an invasive alien plant.
110771.m: Canadian goldenrod is an invasive alien plant.

a: Differences in genetic material within a species
110772.e: Genetic diversity means that the individuals of a species differ in their genes. That is why, for example, not all roe deer are the same.
110772.m: Genetic diversity means differences in genetic material within a species.

110773.q: Why is high genetic diversity important for a species?
110773.e: The more varied the genetic material, the more likely it is that some individuals can cope with diseases or changes in the climate. This lets the species survive.
110773.m: Genetic diversity helps species to adapt to changes.

110774.q: Why are most bananas sold in shops almost genetically identical?
a: They only grow in one country
They are mixed in a laboratory
They have no genes at all
110774.e: The common Cavendish variety is grown from offshoots, so the plants are clones. That is why a fungal disease can threaten whole plantations.
110774.m: Clones without genetic diversity are vulnerable to disease.

110775.q: What is the seed vault on Svalbard for?
a: It stores seeds of crop plants as a reserve
It stores oil for the winter
It measures the temperature at the North Pole
110775.e: Seeds from all over the world are stored in the permafrost on Svalbard. If varieties are lost elsewhere, there is a backup copy here.
110775.m: Seeds are stored in the Svalbard vault as a reserve for the world.

110776.q: What can happen when an animal population is made up of only very few animals?
a: Inbreeding and greater risk of disease
110776.e: When there are only a few animals, they are often closely related. Genetic diversity falls, and inherited diseases or epidemics can have a bigger effect.

110777.q: Which disaster in the 19th century shows how dangerous it can be to grow only a few varieties of potato?
110777.e: From 1845, potato blight destroyed large parts of the harvest in Ireland. Because the same varieties were grown almost everywhere, the disease spread unchecked.
110777.m: Growing only a few varieties makes harvests vulnerable to disease.

110778.q: Which big cat is known for its remarkably low genetic diversity?
110778.e: Cheetahs are genetically very similar, probably because their numbers fell sharply in the past. This makes them more vulnerable to disease.
110778.m: The cheetah has only low genetic diversity.

110779.q: Why are wildlife corridors or wildlife bridges important for genetic diversity?
110779.e: Animals can travel between separate areas using corridors and bridges. This mixes populations and keeps genetic diversity.
110779.m: Wildlife bridges link populations with each other.

110780.q: Which organisation publishes the worldwide Red List of Threatened Species?
110780.e: The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) draws up the worldwide Red List. It assesses how threatened species of animals, plants and fungi are.
110780.m: The IUCN publishes the worldwide Red List.

110781.q: In which country does the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) have its headquarters?
110781.e: The IUCN is based in Gland in the canton of Vaud on Lake Geneva. It was founded in 1948.
110781.m: The IUCN has its headquarters in Switzerland.

110783.q: Which category of the Red List means the highest threat to a species that is still alive?
110783.e: From low to high, the order is: least concern, near threatened, vulnerable, endangered, critically endangered. After that come only the categories for extinct species.
110783.m: “Critically endangered” is the highest level of threat.

110784.q: What does the category “extinct in Switzerland” mean?
a: The species is missing here but lives elsewhere
The species no longer lives anywhere
110784.e: A species can have disappeared from Switzerland but still be found in other countries. This is called regionally extinct.
110784.m: Regionally extinct species still live in other countries.

110785.q: What does the category “near threatened” mean on the Red List?
a: Soon threatened if nothing is done
110785.e: Near threatened species only just fail to meet the criteria for “threatened”. But without protection they could soon slip into a higher category.
110785.m: Near threatened species are close to being threatened.

110945.q: Which part of the human brain is the biggest?
110945.e: The cerebrum makes up by far the biggest part of the human brain and covers the other parts of the brain almost completely.
110945.m: The cerebrum is the biggest part of our brain.

110946.q: What is the outer, heavily folded layer of the cerebrum called?
110946.e: The cerebral cortex is only a few millimetres thick and lies on the outside of the cerebrum.
110946.m: The cerebral cortex forms the outer layer of the cerebrum.

110947.q: Why is the cerebral cortex folded into many ridges and grooves?
a: So that more surface fits inside the skull
So that the brain is lighter
So that knocks are cushioned better
110947.e: Thanks to the folds, a large cortex surface with many nerve cells fits into the limited space of the skull.
110947.m: The folds increase the surface of the cerebral cortex.

110948.q: Which lobe of the cerebrum lies directly behind the forehead?
110948.e: The frontal lobe is the front lobe of the brain and is important for planning, acting and movement.
110948.m: The frontal lobe is at the front, behind the forehead.

110949.q: What does the grey matter of the cerebral cortex mainly consist of?
110949.e: The cell bodies of the nerve cells lie in the grey matter. The white matter underneath consists mainly of nerve fibres with pale myelin sheaths.
110949.m: Grey matter mainly contains the cell bodies of nerve cells.

110950.q: In which lobe of the cerebrum is the auditory cortex?
110950.e: The auditory cortex lies in the temporal lobe, at the side of the head, roughly level with the ears.
110950.m: Hearing is processed in the temporal lobe.

110951.q: In which lobe of the cerebrum are touch sensations from the skin mainly processed?
110951.e: Behind the central groove, in the parietal lobe, lies the somatosensory cortex, which processes touch, pressure and temperature.
110951.m: Touch sensations are processed in the parietal lobe.

110952.q: What job does the motor cortex of the cerebrum do?
110952.e: The motor cortex lies in front of the central groove in the frontal lobe and sends commands for conscious movements to the muscles.
110952.m: The motor cortex starts our conscious movements.

110953.q: Which abilities are mainly linked to the cerebrum?
110953.e: Conscious perception, thinking, language, learning and memory arise in the cerebrum.
110953.m: We think, learn and remember with the cerebrum.

a: At the back of the head below the cerebrum
110954.e: The cerebellum lies in the lower back part of the skull, below the cerebrum and behind the brainstem.
110954.m: The cerebellum sits at the back of the head below the cerebrum.

110955.q: What is the most important job of the cerebellum?
110955.e: The cerebellum makes sure that movements are finely tuned, smooth and balanced.
110955.m: The cerebellum coordinates movements and keeps us balanced.

110956.q: Which test does a doctor use to check whether the cerebellum is working well?
a: Bringing your finger to your nose with your eyes closed
110956.e: For the finger-to-nose test, movements must be precisely coordinated. If the cerebellum is not working properly, you miss your nose or shake.
110956.m: The finger-to-nose test checks the cerebellum.

110957.q: Which skill becomes automatic after lots of practice because the cerebellum has stored the sequence of movements?
110957.e: The cerebellum helps us learn sequences of movements. Practised movements like riding a bike then happen without thinking.
110957.m: The cerebellum helps store practised movements like riding a bike.

110958.q: Which part of the brain is especially busy when you balance on one leg?
110958.e: The cerebellum processes messages from the organ of balance and the muscles. With small corrections it makes sure you do not fall over.
110958.m: The cerebellum works when you balance.

110959.q: Which part of the brain, although it is small, contains most of the brain's nerve cells?
110959.e: The cerebellum contains a huge number of tiny granule cells. That is why it holds well over half of all the nerve cells in the brain.
110959.m: The cerebellum is small but contains the most nerve cells.

110960.q: What is a typical result of damage to the cerebellum?
a: Loss of the sense of smell
110960.e: If the cerebellum is damaged, movements become inaccurate and shaky, and balance is disturbed. This is called ataxia.
110960.m: A damaged cerebellum makes movements unsteady.

110961.q: How many halves does the cerebellum have?
110961.e: The cerebellum has a left and a right half. Between them is a narrow middle part called the vermis.

110962.q: Which vital processes are controlled by the brainstem?
110962.e: The brainstem contains centres that automatically control breathing, heartbeat and blood pressure.
110962.m: The brainstem keeps breathing and the heartbeat going.

110963.q: Which of the following parts belongs to the brainstem?
110963.e: The brainstem includes the midbrain, the pons and the medulla oblongata.
110963.m: The medulla oblongata is part of the brainstem.

110964.q: Which part of the brain leads directly into the spinal cord?
110964.e: The medulla oblongata is the lowest part of the brainstem and leads into the spinal cord at the opening at the base of the skull.
110964.m: The spinal cord begins at the medulla oblongata.

110965.q: What is the bulging part of the brainstem called, through which the cerebrum is connected with the cerebellum?
110965.e: The pons bulges out at the front of the brainstem. Signals from the cerebrum to the cerebellum travel along its nerve pathways.
110965.m: The pons connects the cerebrum with the cerebellum.

110966.q: In which part of the brain are protective reflexes such as coughing, sneezing and swallowing controlled?
110966.e: The centres for coughing, sneezing, swallowing and being sick lie in the medulla oblongata of the brainstem.
110966.m: Coughing and swallowing are controlled in the medulla oblongata.

a: Between the cerebrum and the spinal cord
Low down in the back near the pelvis
Behind the eyes in the nose
110967.e: The brainstem forms the lowest part of the brain. It connects the cerebrum with the spinal cord.
110967.m: The brainstem connects the brain and the spinal cord.

110968.q: Which part of the brain is, among other things, important for whether we are awake or asleep?
110968.e: The brainstem contains a net-like network of nerve cells. Among other things, it controls how awake and alert we are.
110968.m: The brainstem helps to control waking and sleep.

110969.q: What is the thick bundle of fibres connecting the two halves of the cerebrum called?
110969.e: The corpus callosum consists of many millions of nerve fibres and connects the left half of the brain with the right.
110969.m: The corpus callosum connects the two halves of the brain.

110970.q: What is affected in aphasia after a stroke?
110970.e: In aphasia, the language centres in the brain are damaged. People affected have trouble finding words or do not understand what is said.
110970.m: Aphasia is a language disorder caused by brain damage.

110971.q: In which half of the brain are the language centres in most right-handed people?
110971.e: In over 90 percent of right-handed people, the main language centres are in the left half of the brain.
110971.m: In most people, language is processed on the left side of the brain.

110972.q: Which side of the body is often paralysed when a stroke affects the left half of the brain?
a: Only the left side of the face
110972.e: Because the nerve pathways cross over, damage in the left half of the brain leads to paralysis on the right side of the body.
110972.m: A stroke on the left often paralyses the right side of the body.

110973.q: What divides the cerebrum into a left and a right half?
110973.e: A deep groove runs from front to back and separates the two halves of the cerebrum. Lower down they are connected by the corpus callosum.
110973.m: A deep groove separates the two halves of the cerebrum.

110974.q: Which half of the brain controls the movements of the left hand?
110974.e: The nerve pathways cross over on their way to the body. That is why the right half of the brain controls the left side of the body and the other way round.
110974.m: The right half of the brain controls the left side of the body.

110975.q: Why can speech therapy help after a stroke?
a: The brain can form new connections
110975.e: With lots of practice, other parts of the brain can partly take over tasks. That way many people affected learn to speak better again.
110975.m: The brain can form new connections through practice.

110976.q: Do the two halves of the brain work in exactly the same way?
a: No, they partly have different jobs
Yes, they do exactly the same
No, one half is always asleep
110976.e: The two halves of the brain share out some tasks. For example, the language centres are usually in the left half.
110976.m: The two halves of the brain partly have different jobs.

110978.q: Why do we not normally notice the blind spot in our own eye in everyday life?
a: The brain fills in the gap in the picture
The blind spot is too small for light
110978.e: Where the optic nerve leaves the eye there are no sensory cells. The visual system fills in the gap with the surroundings and with the images from the other eye.
110978.m: The brain fills in gaps in the picture that the eye does not provide.

110979.q: What happens in the visual cortex?
a: Signals from the eyes are processed into pictures
110979.e: The eye turns light into electrical signals. Only the visual cortex processes these signals into what we consciously see.
110979.m: The visual cortex turns nerve signals into pictures.

110980.q: Why do we see the world the right way up, even though the image on the retina is upside down?
a: The brain interprets the image correctly
The pupil turns the image round
The tear fluid mirrors the image
110980.e: The lens creates an upside-down image on the retina. Our visual system has learned to interpret this image so that we see up and down correctly.
110980.m: The brain interprets the upside-down retinal image correctly.

110982.q: How do the signals from the eyes reach the visual cortex?
a: Through the optic nerve and visual pathway
110982.e: The retina turns light into nerve signals. These travel along the optic nerve and the visual pathway to the visual cortex at the back of the head.
110982.m: Visual signals travel along the optic nerve and visual pathway to the visual cortex.

110983.q: Why do you sometimes “see stars” after a hard blow to the back of the head?
a: Because the visual cortex there is stimulated
Because the eyes briefly fall out
Because the ears then hear light
110983.e: The visual cortex is at the back of the head. If it is stimulated by a blow, flashes of light appear even though no light is entering the eye.
110983.m: The visual cortex at the back of the head turns signals into pictures.

110984.q: What can damage to both visual cortices cause, even though the eyes are healthy?
