110984.e: Without the visual cortex, the signals from the eyes cannot be processed into pictures. This is called cortical blindness.
110984.m: Without a working visual cortex you are blind, despite healthy eyes.

110985.q: What do many nerve cells in the visual cortex react to especially strongly?
110985.e: Researchers found that cells in the visual cortex react to particular shapes such as edges and lines. From these the brain puts together whole pictures.
110985.m: The visual cortex builds pictures out of edges and lines.

110986.q: What runs through the spinal canal below the end of the spinal cord?
110986.e: Below the spinal cord, only nerve roots continue downwards. Because the bundle looks like a horse's tail, it is called the cauda equina, Latin for horse's tail.
110986.m: Below the spinal cord, only nerve fibres continue.

110987.q: Roughly how long is the spinal cord of an adult?
110987.e: The spinal cord of an adult is about 40 to 50 centimetres long and about as thick as a little finger.
110987.m: The spinal cord is about 45 centimetres long.

110988.q: Where does the spinal cord end in adults?
a: In the lower back, above the pelvis
Right at the bottom in the tailbone
110988.e: The spine grows longer than the spinal cord. That is why the cord ends in the upper lumbar region, and below that only nerve fibres continue.
110988.m: The spinal cord ends in the upper lumbar region.

110989.q: What shape is the grey matter in a cross-section of the spinal cord?
110989.e: In cross-section, the grey matter lies on the inside and looks like a butterfly or an H. The white matter lies around it.
110989.m: The grey matter in the spinal cord looks like a butterfly.

110991.q: Why is cerebrospinal fluid taken with a needle in the lower back?
a: There is no spinal cord there any more
110991.e: The spinal cord ends higher up. If the needle goes in between two lumbar vertebrae, the risk of injuring it is very low.
110991.m: Cerebrospinal fluid is taken in the lower back because the spinal cord no longer runs there.

110992.q: Which fluid surrounds the brain and spinal cord and protects them from knocks?
110992.e: Cerebrospinal fluid bathes the brain and spinal cord like a water cushion and absorbs shocks.
110992.m: Cerebrospinal fluid cushions the brain and spinal cord.

110993.q: What branches off between the vertebrae to the left and right of the spinal cord?
a: Nerves that lead into the body
110993.e: Nerves come out in pairs between the vertebrae. They connect the spinal cord with skin, muscles and organs. Humans have 31 such pairs.
110993.m: Pairs of nerves run from the spinal cord to the whole body.

110994.q: In the knee-jerk reflex, what happens when the doctor taps below the kneecap with the little hammer?
110994.e: The tap briefly stretches the thigh muscle. It contracts as a reflex and straightens the lower leg.
110994.m: In the knee-jerk reflex, the lower leg kicks forwards.

110995.q: Why do many reflexes happen especially quickly?
a: Because they are switched in the spinal cord
Because the muscles are especially big
Because the cerebrum plans them for a long time
Because the blood carries the signals
110995.e: In spinal reflexes, the signal does not have to go to the brain first. The path is short, so the reaction is very fast.
110995.m: A short path through the spinal cord makes reflexes fast.

110996.q: What is at the start of every reflex arc?
a: A sensory receptor that picks up a stimulus
110996.e: A reflex arc begins at the receptor, leads through a sensory nerve pathway to the spinal cord and through a motor pathway to the muscle.
110996.m: Every reflex arc begins with a receptor.

110997.q: In the reflex arc, which nerve cells carry the signal from the spinal cord to the muscle?
110997.e: Sensory nerve cells report the stimulus to the spinal cord. Motor nerve cells carry the command back to the muscle.
110997.m: Motor nerve cells carry the command to the muscle.

110998.q: Which reflex clears the airways when something gets in that should not?
110998.e: If a crumb gets into the windpipe, it triggers a strong cough. That way the foreign object is pushed back out.
110998.m: The cough reflex protects the airways.

110999.q: Which reflex do babies show when you put a finger in their hand?
110999.e: Newborn babies close their hand tightly around anything that touches their palm. This grasp reflex disappears after a few months.

111000.q: Which reflex protects the eye when something suddenly comes towards it fast?
111000.e: In the blink reflex, the eyelids close in a flash and so protect the cornea.
111000.m: The blink reflex protects our eyes.

111002.q: What is part of the peripheral nervous system?
a: The nerves outside the brain and spinal cord
111002.e: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system. All the other nerves in the body belong to the peripheral nervous system.
111002.m: The peripheral nervous system includes all nerves outside the brain and spinal cord.

111003.q: What is the longest and thickest nerve in the human body called?
111003.e: The sciatic nerve runs from the lower back through the buttocks into the leg. At its thickest it is about as thick as a finger.
111003.m: The sciatic nerve is the longest nerve in the body.

111004.q: Which coating around many nerve fibres makes signals travel faster?
111004.e: The myelin sheath insulates the nerve fibre. The signal then jumps from gap to gap and is much faster.
111004.m: The myelin sheath makes nerve fibres faster.

111006.q: What is the long extension of a nerve cell called that passes signals on to other cells?
111006.e: The axon carries signals away from the cell body. The short, branched dendrites, on the other hand, take in signals.
111006.m: The axon carries signals away from the nerve cell.

111007.q: Which muscles can we move at will?
a: The skeletal muscles, for example in the arm
The muscles of the blood vessels
111007.e: We control skeletal muscles consciously through nerves. The heart, gut and blood vessels, on the other hand, work without our will.

111008.q: Which nerve causes the tingling when you knock your “funny bone” at the elbow?
111008.e: The ulnar nerve lies directly under the skin at the elbow. A knock irritates it and causes tingling right down to the little finger.
111008.m: When you hit your funny bone, you knock the ulnar nerve.

111009.q: Roughly how fast do the fastest human nerve fibres carry signals?
a: Up to around 120 metres per second
Up to around 1 metre per second
Up to around 3,000 metres per second
111009.e: Thick nerve fibres with a myelin sheath carry signals at up to about 120 metres per second, which is over 400 kilometres per hour.
111009.m: Fast nerve fibres carry signals at up to 120 metres per second.

111010.q: What is the cranial nerve called that carries signals from the inner ear to the brain?
111010.e: The vestibulocochlear nerve, the nerve for hearing and balance, carries signals from the cochlea and the organ of balance to the brainstem.
111010.m: The vestibulocochlear nerve connects the inner ear with the brain.

111011.q: Which part of the nervous system does the sympathetic nervous system belong to?
111011.e: The autonomic nervous system controls the organs without our will. It consists of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems and the gut nervous system.
111011.m: The sympathetic nervous system is part of the autonomic nervous system.

111012.q: In which situation is the sympathetic nervous system especially active?
111012.e: The sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for action, for example for flight or fight.
111012.m: Under stress, the sympathetic nervous system takes charge.

111013.q: How does the sympathetic nervous system affect the heartbeat?
111013.e: So that muscles get more blood in danger, the sympathetic nervous system raises the heart rate and blood pressure.
111013.m: The sympathetic nervous system makes the heart beat faster.

111014.q: How do the pupils change when the sympathetic nervous system is active?
111014.e: The sympathetic nervous system widens the pupils so that more light enters the eye.
111014.m: Under stress, the pupils get wide.

111015.q: How does the sympathetic nervous system affect digestion?
111015.e: In a dangerous situation, digesting is not important. That is why the sympathetic nervous system slows down the work of the stomach and gut.
111015.m: The sympathetic nervous system slows down digestion.

111016.q: How does the sympathetic nervous system affect the bronchi in the lungs?
111016.e: Wide bronchi let more air into the lungs. That way the body gets enough oxygen during effort.
111016.m: The sympathetic nervous system opens the airways wider.

111017.q: Which hormone does the adrenal medulla release when the sympathetic nervous system is activated?
111017.e: Adrenaline strengthens the effects of the sympathetic nervous system throughout the body, for example a faster pulse.
111017.m: Under stress, the body releases adrenaline.

111018.q: Which part of the nervous system brings back calm and digestion after stress?
111018.e: The sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems work as opposites. The sympathetic steps on the accelerator, the parasympathetic brakes and supports recovery and digestion.
111018.m: The parasympathetic nervous system is the opposite of the sympathetic.

111019.q: When is the parasympathetic nervous system especially active?
111019.e: The parasympathetic nervous system is also called the rest nerve. It looks after recovery and stimulates digestion.
111019.m: The parasympathetic nervous system is at work at rest.

111020.q: How does the parasympathetic nervous system affect the heartbeat?
111020.e: Through the vagus nerve, the parasympathetic nervous system slows the heart. That way it beats more slowly at rest.
111020.m: The parasympathetic nervous system calms the heart.

111021.q: How does the parasympathetic nervous system affect the stomach and gut?
111021.e: The parasympathetic nervous system stimulates the production of digestive juices and the movements of the gut.
111021.m: The parasympathetic nervous system gets digestion going.

111022.q: How does the parasympathetic nervous system change breathing?
a: It becomes faster and more hectic
It has nothing to do with it
111022.e: The parasympathetic nervous system brings calm and recovery. Breathing and heartbeat become slower.
111022.m: The parasympathetic nervous system calms breathing.

111023.q: How do the pupils change under the influence of the parasympathetic nervous system?
111023.e: The parasympathetic nervous system tightens the ring muscle of the iris. This makes the pupil narrower.
111023.m: The parasympathetic nervous system makes the pupils narrow.

111024.q: What happens to the flow of saliva when the parasympathetic nervous system is active?
a: It has nothing to do with it
111024.e: The parasympathetic nervous system prepares the body for digestion. That is why the mouth makes more saliva.
111024.m: The parasympathetic nervous system stimulates the flow of saliva.

111025.q: What is the relationship between the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems called?
111025.e: The two have opposite effects on most organs; for example, one speeds up the heart and the other slows it down.
111025.m: The sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems are opponents.

111026.q: What happens in the brain during an epileptic seizure?
a: Many nerve cells fire at the same time and excessively
A blood vessel in the brain bursts
The brain gets too little sugar
The membranes around the brain become inflamed
111026.e: During a seizure, many nerve cells send signals out of control at the same time. This can lead to jerking movements or loss of awareness.
111026.m: In an epileptic seizure, many nerve cells fire at the same time.

111027.q: What should you never do when another person is having a seizure?
a: Cushion their head with something soft
Time how long the seizure lasts
111027.e: Objects in the mouth can break teeth or block breathing. The right thing is to protect the person from injury and stay with them.
111027.m: During a seizure, nothing should go into the person's mouth.

111028.q: Which organ is affected by epilepsy?
111028.e: Epilepsy is a condition of the brain. An EEG measures brain waves to detect it.
111028.m: Epilepsy is a condition of the brain.

111029.q: What are medicines called that are meant to prevent epileptic seizures?
111029.e: Anti-epileptics make nerve cells less excitable. With them, many people with epilepsy become free of seizures.

111030.q: Which emergency number do you call in Switzerland if a seizure lasts longer than five minutes?
111030.e: 144 is the number of the ambulance service. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade and 1414 the Rega air rescue.
111030.m: In Switzerland you reach the ambulance service on 144.

111031.e: Epilepsy is a condition of the brain and is not passed from person to person.

111032.q: Which stimulus can trigger a seizure in some people with epilepsy?
111032.e: In photosensitive epilepsy, flashing lights or flickering screens can trigger seizures.
111032.m: Flickering light can trigger seizures in some people.

111033.q: What can a small epileptic seizure look like in children?
a: The child stares blankly for a moment and does not react
The child sneezes several times in a row
The child has tummy ache after eating
111033.e: In a so-called absence seizure, the child stares blankly for a few seconds. Then they carry on as if nothing had happened.
111033.m: A short blank stare can be a small seizure.

111035.q: What does a migraine headache typically feel like?
a: Throbbing and often on one side
Slightly pressing all over the head
111035.e: Migraine usually shows itself as a strong, throbbing headache that often affects only one side of the head.
111035.m: Migraine often throbs on one side of the head.

111036.q: Which other complaints often occur with migraine?
111036.e: During an attack, many people feel sick and are sensitive to light and noise.
111036.m: With migraine, light and noise are often bothersome.

111037.q: What are the visual disturbances called, such as flickering or zigzag lines, that sometimes come before a migraine?
111037.e: Some people experience an aura before the headache, usually with flickering or flashes of light in their field of vision.
111037.m: An aura can announce a migraine attack.

111038.q: According to the medical definition, how long does an untreated migraine attack last in adults?
111038.e: According to the international classification of headaches, a migraine attack without treatment lasts 4 to 72 hours.
111038.m: A migraine attack can last up to three days.

111039.q: Who is more often affected by migraine in adulthood?
111039.e: Adult women suffer from migraine about two to three times as often as men.
111039.m: Women get migraines more often than men.

111040.q: What helps many people during a migraine attack?
111040.e: Because light and noise are bothersome, many people go to a quiet, dark room and lie down.
111040.m: Rest and darkness help with migraine.

111041.q: What is a headache diary for in migraine?
111041.e: If you note down attacks, sleep, food and activities, it is easier to see what can trigger a migraine, such as lack of sleep or skipped meals.
111041.m: A headache diary helps to find migraine triggers.

111042.q: Where does the word “migraine” come from?
a: From the Greek word for “half skull”
111042.e: Migraine goes back to the Greek “hemikrania”, which means “half skull”. That fits the pain, which is often on one side.
111042.m: The word migraine originally means “half skull”.

111043.q: Unlike migraine, what does the common tension headache usually feel like?
111043.e: Tension headache is often described as a tight band around the head. It is usually milder than migraine and does not get worse with movement.
111043.m: Tension headache usually presses on both sides of the head.

111330.q: According to the psychologist George Miller, roughly how many units of information can short-term memory hold at once?
111330.e: In 1956 George Miller described the “magical number seven, plus or minus two”. Newer research even suggests it is closer to about four units.
111330.m: Short-term memory can only hold a few things at once.

111332.q: Without repeating it, roughly how long does information stay in short-term memory?
111332.e: Without repetition, information in short-term memory usually fades after about 15 to 30 seconds. After that it is lost unless it has been processed further.
111332.m: Short-term memory forgets quickly if you do not repeat.

111333.q: Which technical term is often used for short-term memory when you actively work with information in it, for example in mental arithmetic?
111333.e: Working memory briefly holds information and processes it at the same time. In mental arithmetic you remember intermediate results and keep calculating with them.
111333.m: In working memory we hold things and work with them at the same time.

111334.q: What happens to most of the things we see and hear but do not pay attention to?
a: They stay in our memory for ever
They go straight into long-term memory
111334.e: Our senses constantly take in a huge amount. Only what we pay attention to reaches short-term memory; the rest is gone after fractions of a second.
111334.m: We can only briefly remember what we pay attention to.

111335.q: What helps most to keep information in short-term memory for longer?
111335.e: Repeating it in your head, for example saying it quietly to yourself, keeps information active. If you get distracted, it is quickly lost.
111335.m: Repeating keeps information alive in short-term memory.

111336.q: Why do you often forget a number straight away if someone speaks to you while you are trying to remember it?
111336.e: Short-term memory has only a little space. New information pushes out the old before it is firmly stored.
111336.m: Distraction pushes information out of short-term memory.

111337.q: Which part of the brain is working memory mainly based in?
111337.e: The front part of the cerebral cortex, the frontal lobe or prefrontal cortex, is especially important for working memory. It also controls planning and attention.
111337.m: The frontal lobe helps us keep things in our head briefly and plan.

111338.q: When does something you have learned get into long-term memory best?
a: When you repeat it several times
When you only skim it once
When you watch TV at the same time
When you forget it again immediately
111338.e: Through repetition, information is activated again and again in the brain. That way it becomes firmly stored and stays for a long time.
111338.m: Repetition brings knowledge into long-term memory.

111339.q: According to the well-known “forgetting curve”, when do we forget most of what we have learned?
a: Never, once you have read it
111339.e: The forgetting curve shows that most is lost in the first hours after learning. Anyone who reviews soon remembers much more.
111339.m: Without repetition, we forget most things soon after learning.

111340.q: According to research, which way of learning works especially well against forgetting?
111340.e: Spaced repetition, with breaks over several days, anchors knowledge better in long-term memory. This is called the spacing effect.
111340.m: If you spread your learning over several days, you remember more.

111341.q: Why do you hardly ever forget how to ride a bike, even if you have not ridden for years?
a: Sequences of movements are stored especially well
Your legs remember the bike themselves
Bikes are always built the same way
You learn it completely new every time
111341.e: The brain stores practised movements like cycling or swimming in a separate area of memory. These skills are hardly ever lost.
111341.m: Practised movements like riding a bike stay stored for a long time.

111342.q: Which memories belong to the personal experiences in long-term memory?
a: What your last birthday was like
What the capital of Switzerland is called
111342.e: We remember our own experiences with place, time and feelings. General knowledge such as arithmetic or capital cities, on the other hand, is stored differently.
111342.m: Personal experiences are stored with place and time.

111343.q: What happens during sleep to what we learned during the day?
a: It only stays in short-term memory.
It is stored in the muscles.
111343.e: During sleep the brain replays what it has learned and strengthens it. That is why enough sleep before a test is important.
111343.m: Good sleep strengthens what we have learned.

111344.q: According to current knowledge, how big is the storage capacity of long-term memory?
111344.e: Unlike short-term memory, long-term memory has no known upper limit, as far as we know today. The problem is more about finding the information again.
111344.m: Long-term memory has a huge amount of space.

111345.q: Why do you remember things better that are linked with strong feelings?
111345.e: The amygdala, the emotion centre, works closely with the hippocampus. That is why emotional experiences are stored more strongly.
111345.m: What moves us stays in our memory better.

111346.q: Which learning method actively tests your own knowledge, for example with flashcards, and so strengthens long-term memory?
111346.e: With active recall, the brain has to work hard to find the answer. This testing effect strengthens knowledge better than simply rereading.
111346.m: Testing yourself strengthens knowledge better than just reading.

111347.q: Which hormone from the adrenal cortex is considered a typical “stress hormone” during long-lasting stress?
111347.e: Cortisol is made in the adrenal cortex and provides the body with energy. If its level stays high for a long time, this can harm your health.
111347.m: Cortisol is an important stress hormone of the body.

111348.q: What is the ancient stress reaction called that prepares the body for fighting or running away?
111348.e: In danger, the body switches in a flash to fight or flight. Pulse, breathing and muscle tension rise.
111348.m: In danger, the body gets ready to fight or run away.

111349.q: What is positive stress called that spurs us on, for example before a competition?
111349.e: We feel eustress as stimulating and motivating. Negative, draining stress is called distress.
111349.m: Positive stress spurs us on, negative stress weighs us down.

111350.e: Stress is how the body and mind respond to pressure, for example before a test. Pulse and breathing get faster and the muscles tense up.
111350.m: Stress is the body's reaction to pressure.

111351.q: Which part of the nervous system becomes active under stress and gets the body ready for action?
111351.e: The sympathetic nervous system is the “accelerator” part of the autonomic nervous system. Afterwards the parasympathetic nervous system brings back calm and recovery.
111351.m: The sympathetic system accelerates, the parasympathetic system brakes.

111352.q: What has been shown to work well for reducing stress?
111352.e: Exercise breaks down stress hormones and lifts your mood. Enough sleep and breaks also help against stress.
111352.m: Exercise is a good remedy for stress.

111353.q: What can long-lasting stress do in the body?
a: The body no longer needs sleep.
111353.e: Stress hormones that stay high for a long time can weaken the body's defences. You then get ill more easily, for example.
111353.m: Constant stress weakens the body's defences.

111354.q: What is it called when your mind suddenly goes blank in a test because of fear?
111354.e: With strong fear, stress hormones temporarily block access to what you have learned. The knowledge is not gone; it is just hard to recall for a moment.
111354.m: In a blackout, knowledge is only blocked for a moment, not lost.

111355.q: What is most likely to help if your mind goes blank in a test?
a: Breathe deeply and do an easier question
Hand in the paper straight away
Read the question again and again
111355.e: Calm breathing lowers the tension. With an easier question you gain confidence, and your memory often comes back.
111355.m: Breathing deeply and starting with something easy helps against a blackout.

111356.q: What are thoughts like “I won't manage it anyway” called, which make test anxiety worse?
111356.e: Negative thoughts make fear stronger. If you replace them with realistic, encouraging sentences, you can become calmer.
111356.m: Encouraging thoughts help against test anxiety.

111357.q: Why does a practice test at home help against test anxiety?
a: You no longer need to study.
Your heart then stops beating altogether.
111357.e: If you practise a test, you know the situation better. Familiar things are less frightening than unknown things.
111357.m: Practising under test conditions takes the fear out of a test.

111358.q: What is a typical physical sign of test anxiety?
111358.e: Before or during the test, your heart can race, your hands can sweat or your tummy can hurt. These are effects of the stress hormones.
111358.m: Test anxiety often shows itself with a pounding heart and sweaty hands.

111359.q: What is the breathing exercise called in which you breathe in slowly through your nose and out even more slowly through your mouth to calm down before a test?
111359.e: In belly breathing, your tummy rises and falls, and breathing out takes longer than breathing in. This calms your pulse and nerves before a test.
111359.m: Slow breathing into your belly calms you before a test.

111360.q: What helps against test anxiety weeks before the test?
a: Making a study plan with fixed stages
Putting everything off until the last day
111360.e: A study plan divides the material into manageable portions. If you know you are well prepared, you go into the test more calmly.
111360.m: An early study plan takes a lot of pressure off a test.

111361.q: In Switzerland, who can you turn to if test anxiety becomes very strong?
a: The teacher or the school psychology service
111361.e: Teachers, parents and the school psychology service can give advice. Strong test anxiety can be tackled well with support.
111361.m: If test anxiety is strong, it is best to get help.

111362.q: What is motivation called that comes from enjoying the thing itself?
111362.e: Intrinsic means “from within”. You do something because it is fun or interesting.
111362.m: If you do something out of enjoyment, you are intrinsically motivated.

111363.q: What is motivation called that comes from reward or punishment from outside?
111363.e: Extrinsic means “from outside”. Examples are marks, money or praise.
111363.m: Rewards from outside create extrinsic motivation.

111364.q: Which messenger substance in the brain plays an important part in the reward system and in motivation?
111364.e: Dopamine is released when we expect a reward. It drives us to pursue a goal.
111364.m: Dopamine drives us to reach goals.

111365.q: Which psychologist is the well-known hierarchy of needs named after?
111365.e: Abraham Maslow arranged human needs in levels that build on each other. Showing them as a pyramid was later made popular by others.
111365.m: The hierarchy of needs comes from Abraham Maslow.

111366.q: What is at the very bottom of Maslow's hierarchy of needs?
111366.e: At the very bottom are needs such as eating, drinking and sleeping. Only when they are met do higher needs come to the fore.
111366.m: Basic needs such as food and sleep form the base of the pyramid.

111367.q: According to research, which kind of goals motivate best?
a: Goals that are as vague as possible
111367.e: Specific and realistic goals show what needs to be done. If you reach small stages, you stay motivated.
111367.m: Clear and achievable goals keep motivation high.

111368.q: What is it called when you keep putting important tasks off until later?
111368.e: Procrastination means “putting off”. It helps to split tasks into small steps and simply get started.
111368.m: If you split tasks into small steps, you put things off less.

111369.q: What can happen if you reward someone for something they enjoy doing anyway?
a: Their inner enjoyment of it can drop.
111369.e: This is called the overjustification effect. Rewards from outside can weaken intrinsic motivation.
111369.m: Too much reward can dampen the enjoyment of something.

111370.q: In psychology, what is the belief called that you can manage a task by your own efforts?
111370.e: The psychologist Albert Bandura coined the term self-efficacy. People who believe in their abilities are more likely to try difficult tasks.
111370.m: If you believe in yourself, you dare to do more.

111371.q: According to Albert Bandura, what makes self-confidence grow most strongly?
111371.e: If you master a challenge yourself, you experience yourself as capable. Such successes strengthen self-confidence the most.
111371.m: Your own successes are the best source of self-confidence.

111372.q: What is the difference between self-confidence and arrogance?
111372.e: Self-confident people trust their own abilities without making others feel small. Arrogance shows itself as acting superior towards others.
111372.m: Real self-confidence does not need arrogance.

111373.q: What is the attitude called that you can improve your abilities through practice?
111373.e: The psychologist Carol Dweck called this attitude a “growth mindset”. Mistakes then count as chances to learn.
111373.m: Mistakes are chances to learn if you believe in growing.

111374.q: Which is more likely to strengthen self-confidence?
111374.e: If you know your strengths, you feel more secure in yourself. Constant comparing, for example on social media, can weaken self-confidence.
111374.m: If you know your strengths, you feel more secure in yourself.

111375.q: What is the value you give yourself as a person called?
111375.e: Self-esteem describes how much you value yourself. It is closely linked with self-confidence.
111375.m: Self-esteem shows how much you value yourself.

111376.q: Which posture generally comes across as self-confident?
a: Standing up straight with eye contact
Hunched over with your head down
Arms in front of your face
Turning away from the other person
111376.e: An upright posture and eye contact come across as confident to others. Body language can also affect how you feel yourself.
111376.m: An upright posture comes across as self-confident.

111377.q: What does being able to say “no” mean for self-confidence?
a: It shows that you respect your own limits.
It shows a lack of self-confidence.
111377.e: If you say no in a friendly but clear way, you take your own needs seriously. That is part of healthy self-confidence.
111377.m: If you know and show your limits, you have healthy self-confidence.

a: Being consciously in the moment without judging
Doing as much as possible at once
111378.e: In mindfulness, you direct your attention to the here and now. Thoughts and feelings are noticed without judging them.
111378.m: Mindfulness means being completely in the moment.

111379.q: What do you mainly train in mindfulness exercises?
111379.e: In mindfulness exercises you learn to rest your attention calmly on something, for example your breath. This can help to reduce stress.

111380.q: Which tradition do mindfulness exercises have their roots in?
111380.e: Mindfulness has its roots in Buddhist meditation practice. Today it is also used without any religious connection.
111380.m: Mindfulness originally comes from Buddhist meditation.

111381.q: What is the exercise called in which you slowly travel through your whole body in your mind?
111381.e: In a body scan, you direct your attention to each part of the body in turn. You feel without changing anything.
111381.m: In a body scan you consciously feel into your whole body.

111382.q: In a simple mindfulness exercise, what do you often focus your attention on?
111382.e: Your breath is always there and works well as an anchor. If your thoughts wander, you calmly return to your breath.
111382.m: The breath is a good anchor for mindfulness.

111383.q: In mindfulness exercises, what should you do when your thoughts wander?
a: Notice it and kindly come back
111383.e: Wandering is completely normal. The exercise is precisely about noticing it and gently bringing your attention back.
111383.m: You kindly bring wandering thoughts back.

111384.q: During which activity can you also practise mindfulness in everyday life?
a: Gaming and chatting at the same time
111384.e: Eating mindfully means consciously noticing the taste, the smell and the chewing. That way an everyday activity becomes an exercise.
111384.m: Eating can also be a mindfulness exercise.

111385.q: According to studies, what effect do regular mindfulness exercises often have?
111385.e: Research shows that mindfulness can reduce stress and improve concentration. Regular practice is important.

111386.q: What is bullying via mobile phones, chats and social networks called?
111386.e: In cyberbullying, people are insulted, humiliated or threatened online. It can go on around the clock and reach many people.
111386.m: Cyberbullying happens online and often does not stop after school.

111388.q: What part do bystanders play in bullying?
a: Stepping in or getting help can stop bullying.
111388.e: Those who watch and stay silent often encourage the bullies. Those who get help or stand by the person affected can make a big difference.
111388.m: Bystanders can stop bullying if they get help.

111389.q: On which short phone number does Pro Juventute offer children and young people in Switzerland advice around the clock?
111389.e: Pro Juventute's number 147 is confidential and free. You can also get help by chat or email, for example with bullying.
111389.m: In Switzerland, the number 147 helps children and young people.

111390.q: What should you do if you are a victim of cyberbullying?
a: Delete everything at once and keep quiet
111390.e: Screenshots save evidence. Then you should involve people you trust and block or report the bullies.
111390.m: With cyberbullying, save evidence and get help.

111391.q: What effect can bullying have on the people affected?
111391.e: Bullying can lead to fear, tummy aches, sleep problems and withdrawing from others. That is why early help is important.
111391.m: Bullying can make people ill and anxious.

111392.q: Which measure is part of a good plan to protect against bullying at schools?
a: Clear class rules and people to turn to
Allowing phones in lessons all the time
111392.e: Clear rules, people to turn to and stepping in quickly help to stop bullying early. The whole school community has a part to play.
111392.m: Clear rules and people to turn to protect against bullying.

111393.q: What is the difference between being alone and loneliness?
a: Loneliness is a painful feeling; being alone is not necessarily.
111393.e: You can enjoy being alone and still feel connected. Loneliness is the painful feeling of having too few real relationships.
111393.m: Being alone is not the same as feeling lonely.

111394.q: How can you tell that someone feels lonely?
a: The person often withdraws and seems sad
The person laughs loudly all the time
111394.e: Lonely people often avoid others and seem down. Asking kindly how they are can help.
111394.m: Withdrawal and sadness can be signs of loneliness.

111395.q: Why can long-lasting loneliness harm your health?
a: It means constant stress for the body.
111395.e: Long-lasting loneliness works like chronic stress. Studies show links with heart and circulation diseases and depression.
111395.m: Long loneliness weighs on body and mind.

111396.q: What can help if you feel lonely?
111396.e: In a club, a sports team or through a hobby, you meet people with the same interests. That is how new friendships begin.

111397.q: According to surveys, which age group, besides older people, feels lonely especially often?
111397.e: Several surveys show that many teenagers and young adults also feel lonely. So loneliness does not only affect older people.
111397.m: Young people often feel lonely too.

111398.q: What is the state called in which someone objectively has hardly any contact with other people?
111398.e: Social isolation describes a measurable lack of contact. Loneliness, on the other hand, is the personal feeling.
111398.m: Social isolation can be measured; loneliness is a feeling.

111399.q: What is a good first step if a classmate often stands alone at break time?
a: Talk to her and invite her to join in
111399.e: A friendly invitation can make a big difference. Often the person is just waiting for someone to talk to them.
111399.m: A friendly word can ease loneliness.

111400.q: Can social media completely replace real contact or cure loneliness?
111400.e: Online contacts can connect people but do not fully replace meeting in person. People who compare themselves a lot can even feel lonelier.
111400.m: Real meetings are especially important against loneliness.

111401.q: What can you do when a friend is sad?
a: Listen and be there for them
111401.e: Good friends listen to each other and are there for each other in difficult times. That often comforts more than lots of words.
111401.m: Listening is a sign of real friendship.

111403.q: How many really close friends do most people have?
111403.e: You can have lots of acquaintances. But really close friendships are usually only a handful.
111403.m: You usually have only a few really close friends.

111404.q: What does it mean when a friend keeps your secret to herself?
111404.e: Someone who keeps a secret shows that they can be trusted. Trust is the basis of every friendship.
111404.m: Trust is the foundation of every friendship.

111406.q: What is a fair way to settle an argument between friends?
a: Say what bothers you using I-statements
Embarrass the other person in front of everyone
Never speak to each other again
111406.e: I-statements such as “I feel left out” describe your own feelings without attacking. That way the conflict can be solved better.
111406.m: I-statements help to settle arguments fairly.

111407.q: What do studies show about the effect of friendships on health?
a: Good relationships support health and well-being.
111407.e: People with stable relationships are on average more content and healthier. Friendships cushion stress.
111407.m: Good friendships are good for body and mind.

111408.q: How can you often recognise an unhealthy friendship?
a: You constantly feel used or put down.
You are allowed to have other friends.
111408.e: In an unhealthy friendship, one side benefits at the other's expense. Then it is fine to keep your distance.
111408.m: A good friendship lets both sides grow.

111409.q: What does resilience mean in psychology?
a: The ability to cope well with crises
111409.e: Resilient people recover after difficult experiences and sometimes grow from them. Resilience can be strengthened.
111409.m: Resilience means getting back up after a crisis.

111410.q: What does the Latin word “resilire”, which resilience comes from, mean?
111410.e: Like a rubber band that springs back, a resilient person finds their feet again after a crisis.
111410.m: Resilience comes from the Latin word for springing back.

111411.q: How is a resilient child most likely to react to a bad mark?
a: They talk about it and try again
They give up the subject for ever
They never try anything new again
111411.e: Resilient children are disappointed too. But they get support and then try again.
111411.m: Resilience means carrying on after setbacks.

111412.q: Which protective factor especially strengthens children's resilience?
a: A stable person they can rely on
111412.e: A reliable person who listens and supports is seen as one of the most important protective factors. This can also be a teacher or a grandparent.
111412.m: A reliable person to turn to makes children strong.

111413.q: What is resilience often compared with as a picture?
a: A roly-poly toy that always stands back up
111413.e: A roly-poly toy rights itself after every push. That is exactly how resilient people are described.
111413.m: Resilient people are like roly-poly toys that always bounce back up.

111414.q: Which attitude is part of high resilience?
a: Giving up when there are problems
111414.e: Resilient people look for solutions and believe they can make a difference. They also get help when they need it.
111414.m: If you look for solutions, you are more resilient.

111415.q: Is resilience something you are born with that never changes?
a: No, it can be strengthened throughout life.
Yes, you are only born with it.
Yes, it is fixed from the age of 6.
111415.e: Resilience comes from the interplay of natural tendencies and experiences. Supportive relationships and challenges you have mastered strengthen it.

111416.q: Which habit can help to strengthen your own resilience?
a: Writing down three good things about the day every evening
111416.e: A gratitude diary turns your attention to the positive. That strengthens confidence and resilience.
111416.m: If you consciously notice good things, you become more resilient.

111417.q: Who is responsible for the school psychology services in Switzerland?
111417.e: In Switzerland, schools are a matter for the cantons. That is why the cantons, sometimes together with municipalities, organise the school psychology services.
111417.m: School psychology services are organised by the cantons.

111418.q: How much does advice from the school psychology service usually cost families?
111418.e: The services of the school psychology service are usually free for pupils and parents. They are paid for with public money.
111418.m: Advice from the school psychology service is usually free.

111419.q: Which learning difficulty can the school psychology service assess, for example?
111419.e: School psychologists assess difficulties with reading and writing, also known as dyslexia. Afterwards they recommend suitable support.
111419.m: The school psychology service assesses learning difficulties.

111420.q: What is the difficulty with maths called that the school psychology service can assess?
111420.e: Dyscalculia means lasting difficulties with calculating and understanding numbers. With support, the difficulties can be reduced.
111420.m: Dyscalculia is a difficulty with maths.

111421.q: Can teenagers also contact the school psychology service themselves?
a: Yes, in many cantons that is possible.
No, only the police can do that.
Yes, but only in the holidays.
111421.e: Referrals often come from parents or teachers. But in many cantons, teenagers can also get in touch directly.
111421.m: Teenagers can also get help from the school psychology service.

111422.q: What applies to conversations with the school psychology service?
a: They are published on the internet.
They are told to the whole class.
They appear in your school report.
111422.e: School psychologists are bound by confidentiality. They only pass on information with consent.
111422.m: What you tell the school psychology service stays confidential.

111423.q: What training do the specialists in the school psychology service usually have?
111423.e: School psychologists usually have a psychology degree specialising in child and adolescent psychology. Many also have further training in school psychology.
111423.m: Trained psychologists work in the school psychology service.

111424.q: What can the school psychology service advise families on, for example?
a: The right time to start school
111424.e: The service advises, for example, on questions about starting school, learning difficulties or behaviour. It supports children, parents and teachers.
111424.m: The school psychology service advises on many school questions.

111425.q: What is a memory aid like “My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming” for the planets called?
111425.e: A mnemonic links something hard to remember with a sentence that is easy to remember. Here the first letters stand for the planets.

111426.q: Where does “Mobbing”, the German word for bullying, come from?
a: From the English “to mob”, meaning to crowd around and harass
From the French “moquer”, meaning to mock
111426.e: The English “to mob” means to jostle or harass. A “mob” is an angry crowd.
111426.m: The German word Mobbing comes from the English “to mob”, to harass.

111427.q: What effect does slight nervousness before a test often have?
a: It helps you to be alert and focused
111427.e: A little tension makes you alert and focused. Too little or too much tension, on the other hand, makes performance worse.
111427.m: A medium level of tension often brings the best performance.

111428.q: What is the state called in which you are completely absorbed in an activity and forget the time?
111428.e: The psychologist Mihály Csíkszentmihályi described flow. It happens when a task is neither too easy nor too difficult.
111428.m: In flow, you forget the time.

111559.q: Why is the butterfly bush (Buddleja) called that?
a: Its flowers attract lots of butterflies.
It only flowers when butterflies are flying.
111559.e: The scented flowers offer plenty of nectar. That is why lots of butterflies often sit on them in summer.
111559.m: Butterflies love the nectar of the butterfly bush.

111560.q: Why does the butterfly bush still do little to help native butterflies?
a: Their caterpillars can hardly eat its leaves.
Its nectar is poisonous to butterflies.
111560.e: The adult butterflies do drink its nectar. But the caterpillars of most native species find no food on it.
111560.m: The butterfly bush is not a food plant for caterpillars.

111561.q: Where does the butterfly bush often grow wild?
a: on railway land and gravel areas
111561.e: It loves warm, open and stony places. That is why you find it on railway land, in gravel pits and on gravel banks of rivers.
111561.m: The butterfly bush likes to settle on stony ground.

111562.q: What should you do if there is still a butterfly bush in your garden?
a: cut off the faded flower heads before the seeds ripen
collect the seeds and give them away
dump the branches in the forest
111562.e: The seeds ripen in the faded flower spikes and are spread by the wind. If you cut the spikes off in time, you stop it spreading.

111563.q: Is the butterfly bush closely related to the real lilac?
a: No, despite its name it is not
Yes, it is a kind of lilac
Yes, it is the wild lilac
111563.e: The butterfly bush's scientific name is Buddleja davidii. It is not closely related to the real lilac of the genus Syringa, though its flowers look similar. In German it is called “summer lilac”.
111563.m: The butterfly bush is not a real lilac.

111564.q: How many seeds can a single butterfly bush produce in a year?
111564.e: One bush produces up to about 3 million tiny seeds. They can stay able to sprout in the soil for a long time.
111564.m: A single butterfly bush can produce millions of seeds.

111565.q: Which flower colour is most common in the butterfly bush?
111565.e: The long, cone-shaped flower heads are usually violet to lilac. Garden varieties also come in white or pink.
111565.m: The butterfly bush usually has purple flowers.

111566.q: Why is ragweed (Ambrosia) dangerous for many people?
111566.e: Ragweed pollen is one of the strongest triggers of allergies. It can cause hay fever and asthma.
111566.m: Ragweed pollen is a strong allergy trigger.

111567.q: Which continent does ragweed come from?
111567.e: Ragweed comes from North America. It spread in Europe mainly during the 20th century.

111568.q: How was ragweed often brought into gardens?
111568.e: Ragweed seeds were often found in seed mixes for birds. They then sprouted underneath bird feeders.
111568.m: Ragweed often came into gardens with bird food.

111569.q: What is the rule for ragweed in Switzerland?
a: It must be reported and removed.
It may be sold as an ornamental plant.
It is grown as a medicinal plant.
111569.e: Anyone who finds ragweed must remove it and report the find. This is meant to stop it spreading in Switzerland.
111569.m: In Switzerland, ragweed must be reported and removed.

111570.q: In which season does ragweed pollen fly?
111570.e: It flowers from about August to October. This makes the pollen season last into autumn for people with allergies.
111570.m: Ragweed makes the pollen season last into autumn.

111571.q: Where does ragweed often grow in our area?
a: On roadsides, building sites and under bird feeders
111571.e: Ragweed likes open, disturbed ground. Under bird feeders it grows from seeds that were in the bird food.
111571.m: Ragweed grows on open ground and under bird feeders.

111572.q: What should you wear when pulling up ragweed?
a: Gloves, and a dust mask when it is flowering
111572.e: The plant sap can irritate the skin. When the plants are flowering, a mask protects you from the allergy-causing pollen.
111572.m: Only pull up ragweed while wearing gloves.

111573.e: Ragweed is pollinated by the wind and produces huge amounts of light pollen grains. These can be carried far through the air.
111573.m: Ragweed pollen is spread by the wind.

111574.q: What makes ragweed pollen especially troublesome?
a: Even very few pollen grains cause symptoms.
It is so big that you can see it.
111574.e: Just a few pollen grains per cubic metre of air can cause symptoms in sensitive people. Other pollen only has an effect in larger amounts.
111574.m: Even tiny amounts of ragweed pollen can trigger allergies.

111575.q: How does cherry laurel get from gardens into forests?
a: Birds eat the fruits and spread the seeds.
The wind carries its leaves away.
Deer carry branches into the forest.
111575.e: Blackbirds and other birds eat the black fruits. Later they drop the seeds somewhere else in their droppings.
111575.m: Birds spread cherry laurel into forests.

111576.q: Which parts of the cherry laurel are especially poisonous?
111576.e: The leaves and seeds contain substances that can turn into poisonous hydrogen cyanide. The fruit flesh is less poisonous, but should not be eaten either.
111576.m: The leaves and seeds of cherry laurel are poisonous.

111577.q: Why is cherry laurel so popular as a hedge plant?
a: It is evergreen and you cannot see through it.
It keeps its flowers in winter.
111577.e: Its leathery leaves stay green all year round. So it gives privacy even in winter.
111577.m: Cherry laurel stays green all year round.

111578.q: Which region does cherry laurel come from?
111578.e: It is native from the Balkans through Asia Minor to the Caucasus. From there it came to Central Europe as an ornamental plant.
111578.m: Cherry laurel comes from south-eastern Europe and western Asia.

111579.q: Why is cherry laurel of little value for native insects?
a: Only a few insects can use it as food.
It kills all insects with scents.
111579.e: Native insects are adapted to native plants. Only a few of them find food on cherry laurel.
111579.m: A cherry laurel hedge offers native insects little food.

111580.q: Since 2024, cherry laurel may no longer be sold in Switzerland. What is the rule for hedges that were planted before?
a: They must be cut down at once
They must be registered with the federal government
They may no longer be trimmed
111580.e: The ban covers selling, giving away and importing. Plants that are already in gardens are not affected.
111580.m: Existing cherry laurel hedges do not have to be removed.

111581.q: Which plant is a native alternative to a cherry laurel hedge?
111581.e: Hornbeam is native to Switzerland and can easily be trimmed into a thick hedge. Its dry leaves often stay on until spring.
111581.m: Native hedge plants are valuable for nature.

111582.q: Which plant is cherry laurel closely related to?
111582.e: Like the sweet cherry, cherry laurel belongs to the genus Prunus. It is not related to the bay laurel, whose leaves are used as a herb.
111582.m: Cherry laurel is a relative of the cherry.

111583.q: Which country does the tree of heaven come from?
111583.e: The tree of heaven is native to China. It was brought to Europe in the 18th century.
111583.m: The tree of heaven originally comes from China.

111584.q: Apart from seeds, how does the tree of heaven reproduce?
111584.e: New shoots keep growing from its roots. This creates dense groups of young trees.
111584.m: The tree of heaven grows new trees from its roots.

111585.q: What often happens if you simply cut down a tree of heaven?
a: It sprouts strongly again from the stump and roots.
It turns into a shrub without leaves.
111585.e: After it is cut down, it forms lots of new shoots. That is why special methods are needed to control it.
111585.m: Simply cutting down a tree of heaven encourages new shoots.

111586.q: For which kind of animal farming was the tree of heaven also planted in Europe in the 19th century?
111586.e: Its leaves were food for the ailanthus silkmoth. People wanted to make silk with this caterpillar.
111586.m: The tree of heaven was once food for silkworms.

111587.q: How does the tree of heaven hold back the growth of other plants?
a: It releases inhibiting substances into the soil.
It shades them only at night.
111587.e: Its roots and leaves contain substances that stop other plants from sprouting and growing. This effect is called allelopathy.
111587.m: The tree of heaven fights its neighbours with chemicals.

111588.q: What do you notice when you crush the leaves of a tree of heaven?
111588.e: Crushed leaves give off an unpleasant smell. The male flowers also smell strong.
111588.m: Tree of heaven leaves smell unpleasant when crushed.

111589.q: Why does the tree of heaven cope well in cities?
a: It can stand heat, drought and poor soil.
It only grows in clean mountain air.
It needs fresh spring water every day.
111589.e: It even grows in cracks in walls, on railway land and on wasteland. There it has little competition.
111589.m: The tree of heaven is a tough city dweller.

111590.q: What do the fruits of the tree of heaven look like?
111590.e: The seeds sit in long, twisted wings. This lets the wind carry them away.
111590.m: The tree of heaven has winged fruits.

111591.q: What is the rule for the tree of heaven in Switzerland today?
a: It may no longer be planted.
It has been declared the national tree.
It must stand in every park.
111591.e: The tree of heaven is listed in Annex 2.1 of the Release Ordinance. It may no longer be sold, planted or propagated; the only thing allowed is to control it.
111591.m: In Switzerland you may no longer plant the tree of heaven.

111592.q: Which continent does annual fleabane come from?
111592.e: Annual fleabane is native to North America. In Europe it was first grown as an ornamental plant.
111592.m: Annual fleabane comes from North America.

111593.q: Which native flower is annual fleabane often confused with because of its flowers?
111593.e: It has white ray petals around a yellow centre, like the ox-eye daisy. But its flower heads are much smaller.
111593.m: Annual fleabane looks like a small ox-eye daisy.

111594.q: What is special about the way annual fleabane makes seeds?
a: The seeds form even without pollination.
It needs two plants to do it.
It only makes seeds every ten years.
The seeds grow in the roots.
111594.e: It can make seeds without fertilisation. That is why even a single plant produces lots of seeds that can sprout.
111594.m: Annual fleabane needs no pollinators for its seeds.

111595.q: Despite its name, what is true about how long annual fleabane lives?
a: It can also live for two years.
It always lives only a few weeks.
It always lives exactly one month.
It lives for several hundred years.
111595.e: It often survives the winter as a rosette of leaves and only flowers in the second year. So it lives for one or two years.
111595.m: Annual fleabane often lives longer than a year.

111596.q: What is the most effective way to get rid of annual fleabane?
a: pull it up with its roots before it flowers
111596.e: Its roots are shallow, so it is easy to pull up. If you remove it with its roots before it flowers, it can neither grow back nor make seeds.
111596.m: Pull up fleabane by the roots before it flowers.

111597.q: Why does mowing alone do little against annual fleabane?
a: It sprouts again and flowers once more.
111597.e: After cutting, it grows new stems from its base and soon flowers again, often lower down. So it still makes seeds.

111598.q: In which habitats does annual fleabane spread especially well?
a: in meadows, on roadsides and wasteland
111598.e: It loves open, sunny areas. That is why you find it in meadows, on roadsides, on embankments and on wasteland.
111598.m: Annual fleabane likes sunny, open places.

111599.q: Where does the German name “Berufkraut” for fleabane probably come from?
a: from the belief that it protects against being bewitched
from its use in vocational schools
111599.e: In the past, the German word “berufen” meant something like “to bewitch”. People believed that plants of this genus protected against spells.
111599.m: The German name Berufkraut comes from old folk beliefs.

111600.q: What do you call plants from distant countries that spread strongly here and cause damage?
111600.e: Neophytes are plants that people have brought in from elsewhere. They are called invasive when they spread strongly and push out native species.
111600.m: Invasive neophytes spread strongly and push out native plants.

111601.q: What does the Swiss Release Ordinance regulate?
a: how organisms are handled in the environment
the opening hours of garden centres
111601.e: Its full title is “Ordinance on the Handling of Organisms in the Environment”. This also covers invasive non-native plants.
111601.m: The Release Ordinance regulates how organisms are handled in the environment.

111602.q: What are you allowed to do with banned invasive plants such as Himalayan balsam?
a: Grow more of them in the garden
111602.e: Any handling of banned invasive plants is forbidden, such as selling, giving away and planting. The only thing allowed is getting rid of them.
111602.m: With banned invasive species, only getting rid of them is allowed.

111603.q: Which palm may no longer be sold in Switzerland because it grows wild in the forests of southern Switzerland?
111603.e: The Chinese windmill palm is often called the Ticino palm and is spreading in the forests of Ticino. That is why it may no longer be passed on to others or imported.
111603.m: The Ticino palm is really an invasive windmill palm from Asia.

111604.q: Who in Switzerland is mainly responsible for enforcing the bans on invasive plants?
111604.e: The federal government makes the rules and the cantons put them into practice. Only import controls are the federal government's job.
111604.m: The cantons make sure the bans on neophytes are followed.

111605.q: Why are invasive plants a problem for nature?
a: They turn the soil into sand
111605.e: Invasive plants often grow fast and thick. They take light and space from native plants, and animals lose their food too.
111605.m: Invasive plants push out native species.

111606.q: Where should invasive plants go once they have been pulled up?
a: In the household rubbish, not on the compost
At the edge of the forest
111606.e: On the compost or out in nature, seeds and pieces of root can keep growing. Household rubbish is burnt, so they can no longer spread.
111606.m: Invasive plants go in the household rubbish.

111607.q: Why do customs officers check whether banned plants are being brought into Switzerland?
a: So that no more invasive species enter the country
So that garden centres sell more
So that there are more bees
111607.e: Many invasive plants come into the country through trade. Checks at the border are meant to stop new problem plants being brought in.
111607.m: Customs helps keep invasive plants out.

a: A plant brought in from elsewhere that spreads strongly and causes harm
A native plant that is threatened with extinction
A plant that only grows high in the mountains
A new vegetable variety from the garden centre
111608.e: Neophytes are plants that were brought to us from other parts of the world. They are called invasive when they spread strongly and push out native plants or cause other damage.
111608.m: Invasive neophytes are introduced plants that spread and cause harm.

111609.q: Which plants were on the Black List?
111609.e: The Black List contained invasive neophytes whose damage had been proven. Their spread was to be stopped.
111609.m: The Black List contained harmful invasive neophytes.

111610.q: Why should you not plant invasive neophytes such as the butterfly bush in your garden?
111610.e: Invasive neophytes spread from gardens into nature. There they take space and light from native plants.
111610.m: Invasive neophytes push out native plants.

111611.q: What kinds of damage were considered when adding a plant to the Black List?
a: to biodiversity, health or the economy
111611.e: A species went on the list if it harmed nature, people or the economy. This includes things like allergies or damage to riverbanks.
111611.m: The Black List considers damage to nature, health and the economy.

111612.q: Which of these plants was on Switzerland's Black List?
111612.e: Giant hogweed comes from the Caucasus and is invasive. The much smaller common hogweed, on the other hand, is native.
111612.m: Giant hogweed is an invasive neophyte.

111613.q: How do you correctly dispose of invasive neophytes pulled up in the garden?
a: In the household rubbish, not on the compost
On the compost heap in the garden
In the stream behind the house
111613.e: On the compost, seeds and pieces of root can survive and keep spreading. That is why invasive neophytes belong in the household rubbish, which is burnt.
111613.m: Invasive neophytes belong in the household rubbish, not on the compost.

111614.q: What is the counterpart to the Black List called, which lists threatened native species?
111614.e: The Red List shows which species are threatened or close to extinction. The Black List, on the other hand, names harmful non-native species.
111614.m: The Red List names threatened species.

111615.q: Why should flowering neophytes not go on the garden compost?
a: Their seeds can survive and spread.
They make the compost too acidic.
111615.e: Garden compost often does not get hot enough to kill all the seeds. They would then be spread again with the compost.
111615.m: Seeds of neophytes belong in the household rubbish.

111616.q: Why is it worth tackling neophytes early?
a: Small patches can still be removed completely.
Large patches disappear on their own.
111616.e: As long as there are only a few plants, getting rid of them is easy and cheap. Removing large patches takes many years and costs a lot.
111616.m: The earlier you tackle neophytes, the easier it is.

111617.q: Why must you protect your skin when tackling giant hogweed?
a: Its sap causes burns in sunlight.
It turns your skin green for ever.
111617.e: The sap contains substances that make the skin sensitive to light. In sunlight, painful blisters appear, like a burn.
111617.m: Only touch giant hogweed while wearing protective clothing.

111618.q: Why must areas be checked for several years after neophytes have been removed?
a: Seeds in the soil can still sprout years later.
The law requires mowing every day.
111618.e: The soil often holds a store of seeds that can still sprout, called the seed bank. New plants grow from it even years later.
111618.m: With neophytes you need patience and follow-up checks.

111619.q: What can you do in your own garden to stop neophytes spreading?
a: scatter seeds of exotic plants in the forest
throw garden waste into the stream
111619.e: Native plants do not spread invasively and provide food for many animals. This makes a nature-friendly garden.
111619.m: Native garden plants are good for nature.

111620.q: Why are herbicides rarely used to control neophytes?
a: They also harm other plants and waters.
They only work on native plants.
111620.e: Weedkillers also hit plants you want to keep and can get into the water. That is why they are only used in exceptional cases and by experts.
111620.m: With neophytes, pulling up and mowing come before poison.

111621.q: What is the best way to remove young seedlings of invasive trees and shrubs?
a: pull them up with their roots
111621.e: Small seedlings can still easily be pulled out of the ground with their roots. Later the roots hold firm and sprout again after being cut.
111621.m: It is best to pull up young woody plants with their roots.

111622.q: What happens to a tree if you remove a ring of bark all the way round it?
111622.e: Sap carrying nutrients flows under the bark. If the bark is removed all the way round, this flow of sap is cut off and the tree slowly dies. This is one way to control invasive trees, for example.
111622.m: Without a ring of bark all round, a tree slowly dies.

111716.q: What is the main job of phagocytes in the body?
111716.e: Phagocytes surround bacteria, dead cells and foreign substances and break them down inside themselves. In this way they clear away intruders and cell remains.
111716.m: Phagocytes swallow germs and break them down.

111717.q: Where in the body are phagocytes found?
a: In the blood and in the tissues
111717.e: Phagocytes travel in the blood and move into the tissues when needed. There they eat germs and cell remains.
111717.m: Phagocytes patrol the blood and tissues.

111718.q: Apart from germs, what else do phagocytes eat?
111718.e: Phagocytes also clear away dead cells and cell debris. They are the body's cleaning team.
111718.m: Phagocytes also clear away cell remains.

111719.q: How does a phagocyte make a germ harmless?
a: It surrounds it and digests it
It stabs it with a spike
It flushes it out of the body
111719.e: The phagocyte wraps its outer layer around the germ and encloses it in a little bubble. There it is broken down by enzymes.

111720.q: Which group of blood cells do phagocytes belong to?
111720.e: Phagocytes are part of the white blood cells, the leukocytes. These cells are responsible for defence.

111721.q: Why is there often pus when a wound is infected?
a: It is made of dead defence cells and germs
It is fat that has leaked out
111721.e: Pus contains many white blood cells that have fought against the germs, along with germs and cell remains.
111721.m: Pus shows that defence cells have been fighting.

111722.q: How do phagocytes work together with other defence cells?
a: They show them parts of the germ
They eat the other defence cells
111722.e: Phagocytes display fragments of the germs they have eaten on their surface. That way other defence cells recognise the enemy and can fight it in a targeted way.

111723.q: Where do phagocytes move to when bacteria multiply in a wound?
a: Out of the blood into the wound
111723.e: With inflammation, phagocytes leave the blood vessels and move to the wound. There they eat the bacteria.

111724.q: Which body fluid is filtered in the lymph nodes?
111724.e: Lymph is a pale fluid from the tissues. On its way back into the blood, it flows through lymph nodes, which filter out germs.

111725.q: Why do lymph nodes often swell during an infection?
a: Because defence cells multiply strongly there
Because they store water for later
111725.e: When defence cells in the lymph node recognise a germ, they multiply quickly. This makes the lymph node bigger and sometimes tender.
111725.m: Swollen lymph nodes show that the body's defences are working.

111726.q: Where can you often easily feel swollen lymph nodes when you have a cold?
a: On the top of the foot
111726.e: There are many lymph nodes in the neck that filter the lymph from the head and throat. That is why you can often feel them when you have a cold.
111726.m: With a sore throat, the lymph nodes in the neck are often swollen.

111727.q: Roughly how many lymph nodes does an adult have?
111727.e: A person has around 600 to 700 lymph nodes. Many of them are in the neck, the armpits, the groin and the abdomen.
111727.m: Humans have a few hundred lymph nodes.

111728.q: Which defence cells are found in especially large numbers in the lymph nodes?
111728.e: Lymphocytes, that is B cells and T cells, gather in the lymph nodes. There they meet germs and are activated.
111728.m: In lymph nodes, many lymphocytes wait for germs.

111729.q: Which organ system do the lymph nodes belong to?
111729.e: Lymph nodes, lymph vessels and the spleen belong to the lymphatic system. It mainly serves defence and the removal of tissue fluid.
111729.m: Lymph nodes are part of the lymphatic system.

111730.q: What shape are lymph nodes typically?
111730.e: Lymph nodes are usually bean-shaped and a few millimetres to about one centimetre in size. They are embedded in the tissue.
111730.m: Lymph nodes look like small beans.

111731.q: What are the vessels called that bring lymph to the lymph nodes?
111731.e: Lymph vessels collect fluid from the tissues and lead it through the lymph nodes. Finally, the lymph flows into the veins.
111731.m: Lymph vessels carry lymph through the lymph nodes.

a: At the back of the throat on each side
At the top of the nasal cavity
Low down in the voice box
111732.e: The tonsils lie on the left and right between the arches of the palate, where the mouth meets the throat. You can see them when you open your mouth wide.
111732.m: The tonsils sit on the left and right at the back of the throat.

111733.q: What do you often feel especially strongly with tonsillitis?
a: A stabbing pain in the knee
111733.e: The inflamed tonsils are swollen and red. That is why swallowing hurts most of all, and there is often a fever too.
111733.m: Tonsillitis gives you a sore throat when swallowing.

111734.q: Why are tonsils sometimes removed in an operation?
a: Because they get inflamed very often
Because they push the teeth out of place
111734.e: If someone gets tonsillitis very often, their tonsils can be taken out. The body still has plenty of other defence cells.
111734.m: If they get inflamed very often, the tonsils are sometimes removed.

111735.q: How many tonsils (palatine tonsils) does a person normally have?
111735.e: There is one tonsil on the left and one on the right side of the throat. There are also other tonsils, such as the adenoids.

111736.q: What job do the tonsils do?
a: Recognising germs from the mouth and nose early
Controlling the pitch of the voice
111736.e: The tonsils are made of lymphatic tissue. They come into contact early with germs from the air we breathe and from food, and they trigger a defence.
111736.m: The tonsils are guards at the entrance to the mouth and throat.

111737.q: What kind of tissue are the tonsils mainly made of?
111737.e: The tonsils contain a great many defence cells. That is why they belong to the immune system and help to recognise germs early.
111737.m: The tonsils are made of defence tissue.

111738.q: What are enlarged adenoids in children commonly called in German, even though it is not quite correct?
111738.e: Enlarged adenoids can make breathing through the nose difficult. In everyday German they are called “polyps”, even though they are not real polyps.
111738.m: Enlarged adenoids are often called polyps.

111739.q: What does the doctor use to treat tonsillitis caused by bacteria?
111739.e: Antibiotics work against bacteria. They do not help against viruses, so the doctor often first does a test to see which germs are the cause.
111739.m: Antibiotics help against bacteria, not viruses.

a: A defence reaction of the body to something harmful
A special kind of broken bone
An inherited disease you are born with
111740.e: Inflammation happens when the body reacts to germs, injuries or foreign substances. It is meant to limit the damage and start healing.
111740.m: Inflammation is a protective reaction of the body.

111741.q: What is inflammation called that lasts for months or even years?
111741.e: Acute inflammation starts suddenly and usually dies down after a few days. If it lasts a long time, it is called chronic inflammation.

111742.q: Which is NOT a typical sign of inflammation?
111742.e: Typical signs of inflammation are redness, warmth, swelling, pain and limited function. The spot becomes warm, not cold.
111742.m: Inflamed spots are red, warm, swollen and painful.

111743.q: Why does an inflamed spot become warm?
a: Because more blood flows to it
Because the skin there gets thinner
111743.e: With inflammation, the blood vessels widen. More warm blood flows into the area, which therefore feels warm.
111743.m: More blood flow makes inflamed spots warm.

a: Because fluid leaks from the blood vessels into the tissue
Because air gets under the skin
Because the muscles there get thicker
111744.e: The walls of the small blood vessels become leakier. Fluid and defence cells get into the tissue, which makes it swell.
111744.m: Leaking fluid makes inflamed tissue swell.

111745.q: Which ending do many medical names for inflammations have?
111745.e: Examples are bronchitis and arthritis. The ending “-oma”, on the other hand, often stands for a growth, and “-algia” for pain.

111746.e: The ending “-itis” stands for inflammation. In bronchitis, the branches of the windpipe are inflamed.
111746.m: Bronchitis is an inflammation of the bronchi.

111747.q: Which cells move into the tissue during inflammation to fight germs?
111747.e: White blood cells are part of the body's defences. During inflammation they move out of the blood vessels into the tissue and fight germs.
111747.m: White blood cells fight germs during inflammation.

111748.q: Why does an inflamed spot often hurt?
a: Messenger substances and the swelling irritate the pain nerves
111748.e: During inflammation, messenger substances are released and the tissue swells. Both irritate the nerves, which is why the spot hurts.

111749.q: What is pus mainly made of?
a: Dead defence cells, germs and bits of tissue
Fat and oil from the skin
111749.e: Pus forms when many defence cells die while fighting bacteria. Together with germs and broken-down tissue they form a thick fluid.
111749.m: Pus is mainly made of dead defence cells.

111750.q: What is an enclosed collection of pus in a newly formed cavity in the tissue called?
111750.e: In an abscess, tissue is broken down and a cavity full of pus forms. A haematoma, on the other hand, is a bruise.
111750.m: An abscess is a cavity of pus in the tissue.

111751.q: What is a pus-filled inflammation of a hair follicle and the area around it called?
111751.e: A boil usually develops from bacteria that get into a hair follicle. A painful, pus-filled lump forms.
111751.m: A boil is an inflamed, pus-filled hair follicle.

111752.e: Pus is usually yellowish to greenish and cloudy. The colour comes from the many cells and their parts.
111752.m: Pus is usually yellowish and cloudy.

111753.q: Which bacteria are among the most common causes of pus?
111753.e: Staphylococcus aureus is one of the main causes of pus-filled skin and wound infections. Lactic acid bacteria, on the other hand, are used for yoghurt, for example.

111754.q: Why should you not squeeze a pus-filled spot with dirty fingers?
111754.e: When you squeeze, bacteria can get deeper into the tissue. Then the inflammation can get bigger.
111754.m: It is better not to squeeze pus-filled spots.

111755.q: Which cells fight bacteria during inflammation and form pus in the process?
111755.e: White blood cells move to the inflammation and eat bacteria. Many die in the process and form pus together with the germs.
111755.m: Pus forms from dead white blood cells.

111756.q: What is a small blister on the skin filled with pus called?
111756.e: A pustule is a pus blister, as found in acne, for example. A papule is a small bump without pus.
111756.m: A pustule is a pus blister.

111757.q: What job do the memory cells of the immune system do?
a: Recognise a germ again and fight it quickly
111757.e: Memory cells stay in the body after an infection. If they meet the same germ again, they immediately start a strong defence.
111757.m: Memory cells remember germs that were fought before.

111758.q: Which blood cells do memory cells belong to?
111758.e: White blood cells are the body's defence cells. Memory cells are a special kind of them.
111758.m: Memory cells are white blood cells.

111759.q: Why do you usually get chickenpox only once in your life?
a: Memory cells recognise the virus the next time
The virus only occurs in children
The skin becomes impenetrable with age
The virus dies out in summer
111759.e: After the first illness, long-lasting immunity remains. Memory cells make sure that a new infection is usually fought off without any signs of illness.
111759.m: Anyone who has had chickenpox is usually protected for life.

111760.q: How does a vaccination make use of memory cells?
a: The body makes them without really getting ill
It kills all the old memory cells
It turns memory cells into red blood cells
It prevents memory cells from forming
111760.e: A vaccine contains weakened or killed germs or parts of them. The immune system reacts to them and creates memory cells.
111760.m: A vaccination trains the immune memory.

111761.q: Where in the body are the white blood cells made from which memory cells develop?
111761.e: All blood cells, including white blood cells, are made in the red bone marrow. Some of them later become memory cells.
111761.m: Defence cells are made in the bone marrow.

111762.q: How long can some memory cells survive in the body?
111762.e: Many memory cells are very long-lived. That is why getting over an illness or having a vaccination often protects you for a very long time.
111762.m: Memory cells can live for decades.

111763.q: How does the immune system react the second time it meets the same germ?
a: Exactly the same as the first time
111763.e: The first time, the defences need a few days. The second time, the memory cells recognise the germ immediately and the defence starts faster and more strongly.
111763.m: The second time, the body defends itself faster.

111764.q: What does a booster vaccination do?
a: It raises the number of memory cells and antibodies again
It replaces the making of red blood cells
111764.e: With some vaccinations, the protection fades over time. Another dose refreshes the immune memory.
111764.m: A booster vaccination strengthens the immune memory.

111765.q: What kind of organ is the thymus?
111765.e: Defence cells are trained in the thymus. So it serves the body's defence, not digestion, the senses or excretion.
111765.m: The thymus is an organ of the immune system.

111766.q: Which defence cells mature in the thymus?
111766.e: In the thymus these cells are trained and mature into working defence cells. They are also named after this organ.
111766.m: T cells mature in the thymus.

111767.q: What would happen if a child were born without a working thymus?
111767.e: Without a thymus, no mature T cells can form. The body then lacks an important part of its defences, and infections become very dangerous.
111767.m: Without a thymus, the body lacks an important part of its defences.

111768.q: How does the thymus change over the course of life?
a: It shrinks and partly turns into fatty tissue
It keeps growing into old age
It turns to bone and becomes a rib
It moves from the chest into the abdomen
111768.e: The thymus is large and active in children. In adults it gets smaller and smaller and is mostly replaced by fat.

111769.q: Where do the immature precursor cells come from that mature in the thymus?
111769.e: All blood cells are made in the bone marrow. Some of the precursors of the lymphocytes travel from there through the blood to the thymus.
111769.m: The precursors of the thymus cells come from the bone marrow.
