112325.q: What is the name of the Swiss foundation that supports mountain farming families with donations?
112325.e: Swiss Mountain Aid funds projects in mountain areas, such as new barns or paths. This helps people keep living in the mountains.
112325.m: Swiss Mountain Aid supports people in mountain areas.

112326.q: Which job do many mountain farmers still do by hand with a rake, because machines cannot drive on steep slopes?
112326.e: In very steep places, mountain farmers have to rake the hay by hand and sometimes even carry it. This work is tiring and takes a lot of time.
112326.m: On steep slopes, hay is often still raked by hand.

112327.q: Which important task do mountain farmers carry out besides producing food?
a: They look after the cultural landscape
112327.e: By mowing and grazing, mountain farmers stop meadows from becoming overgrown with bushes and forest. This protects meadows rich in species and keeps the landscape for tourism and nature.
112327.m: Mountain farmers keep the mountain landscape open with their work.

112328.q: How do some mountain farmers get hay or milk across steep ground down to the valley?
a: With a lorry across the pasture
112328.e: Where there is no road, small cableways carry goods over gorges and slopes. They save many hours of walking.
112328.m: A goods cableway helps mountain farmers move things.

112329.q: What is the custom in the Justistal valley (Canton of Bern) called, where the Alpine cheese is shared among the farmers in autumn?
112329.e: At the Chästeilet, the cheese made in summer is shared out fairly. Each farmer gets as much cheese as his cows gave milk.
112329.m: At the Chästeilet, the Alpine cheese is shared among the farmers.

112330.q: What is the milk heated in to make cheese on the Alpine pasture?
112330.e: The cheese cauldron is a large pot, often made of copper, that hangs over the fire. In it, the milk is warmed and thickened with rennet.
112330.m: On the Alpine pasture, milk is made into cheese in a copper cauldron.

112331.q: Who owns many Swiss Alpine pastures together?
112331.e: Many Alpine pastures belong to cooperatives, corporations or municipalities. Members may graze their animals there in summer and share the work.
112331.m: Many Alpine pastures are used jointly by cooperatives.

112332.q: Which prayer call does the cheesemaker speak or sing through a funnel in the evening on some Alpine pastures?
112332.e: The Alpine blessing (Alpsegen), also called the prayer call, is meant to protect animals and people on the pasture during the night. It is spoken mainly in Catholic Alpine areas.
112332.m: With the Alpine blessing, the cheesemaker asks for protection for the pasture.

112333.q: What is the festive procession called when the animals go up to the Alpine pasture in early summer?
112333.e: In the Alpine ascent, farmers walk up to the pasture with cows, goats and sheep. In autumn they return with the Alpine descent.
112333.m: The Alpine summer begins with the Alpine ascent.

112334.q: Which animals did people use to keep on many Alpine pastures to feed them the whey from cheesemaking?
112334.e: Making cheese leaves lots of whey. On many Alpine pastures it was used to fatten pigs, so nothing went to waste.
112334.m: Alpine pigs used to make use of the whey from cheesemaking.

112335.q: What is the building on the Alpine pasture called, where cheese is made and the staff live?
112335.e: The cheese cauldron and cheese press are in the cheesemaker's hut. Often the cheesemaker and herders also live there during the Alpine summer.
112335.m: Cheese is made in the cheesemaker's hut on the Alpine pasture.

112336.q: What do the animals on the Alpine pasture mainly eat?
112336.e: On the Alpine pasture, the animals graze the natural meadows. These are rich in herbs and flowers.
112336.m: On the Alpine pasture, the animals eat fresh mountain grass and herbs.

a: The animals spend the summer on the Alpine pasture
The animals sleep in the barn in summer
The hay is sold in summer
The farmers go on holiday to the sea in summer
112337.e: In summer grazing, cows, cattle, sheep and goats go up to the Alpine pastures in summer. In autumn they return to the valley.
112337.m: In summer grazing, the animals graze on the Alpine pasture in summer.

112338.q: Roughly how long does an Alpine summer last in Switzerland?
112338.e: The Alpine season usually starts in June and ends in September. So it lasts about 100 days.
112338.m: An Alpine summer lasts about 100 days.

112339.q: What advantage does summer grazing have for the farm in the valley?
a: More winter feed can be harvested in the valley
The cows give more milk in the valley
No barn is needed in the valley any more
The valley is no longer mown
112339.e: While the animals are on the Alpine pasture, meadows for hay and silage grow in the valley. The animals need this feed in winter.
112339.m: Summer grazing saves feed in the valley for the winter.

112340.q: Which animals do herders use on Swiss Alpine pastures to protect the sheep from wolves?
112340.e: Livestock guardian dogs live with the flock of sheep and drive wolves away. Hikers should not disturb them and should walk calmly past the flock.
112340.m: Livestock guardian dogs guard the sheep on the Alpine pasture.

112341.q: Why is summer grazing important for biodiversity?
a: Grazed Alpine pastures become less overgrown with bushes
The animals eat up all the flowers
It fertilises the pastures like fields
112341.e: Without grazing, bushes and later forest grow on many Alpine pastures. Open Alpine meadows give many flowers and insects a place to live.
112341.m: Grazing animals keep Alpine pastures open and rich in species.

112342.q: Apart from cattle, which animals spend the summer on Swiss Alpine pastures especially often?
112342.e: Besides cows and cattle, lots of sheep spend the summer in the mountains. Sheep can graze even on very steep ground.
112342.m: In summer, sheep often graze high up in the mountains.

112343.q: In which month do the animals in Switzerland usually go up to the Alpine pasture?
112343.e: When the snow has melted and the grass is growing, the Alpine ascent begins. This is usually in June.
112343.m: The animals usually go up to the Alpine pasture in June.

112344.q: What decides how many animals may spend the summer on an Alpine pasture?
a: How much food the pasture provides
The size of the cheesemaker's hut
112344.e: Each Alpine pasture has a fixed number of animals that matches how much grass grows. This way the pasture is not overused and stays healthy.
112344.m: Only as many animals may graze on a pasture as the grass can feed.

112345.q: Which plants may not be grown in organic farming?
112345.e: Organic farming completely bans genetic engineering, including in animal feed. Organic farmers use normal seed or seed bred organically.
112345.m: Genetic engineering is banned in organic farming.

112346.q: What do organic farmers mainly use to fertilise their fields?
112346.e: Farm fertilisers such as manure, slurry and compost return nutrients to the soil. This creates a cycle on the farm.
112346.m: Organic farmers fertilise with manure and compost.

112347.q: Which canton has the highest share of organic farms?
112347.e: In the Grisons, more than half of the farms are run organically. Many mountain farms keep animals on meadows and need few sprays.
112347.m: The Grisons is Switzerland's organic canton.

112348.q: Which symbol can you find on many organic products in Switzerland?
112348.e: The Bud (Knospe) is the label of Bio Suisse. The IP-Suisse ladybird stands for environmentally friendly but not organic production.
112348.m: The Bud is the best-known organic label in Switzerland.

112349.q: What is the rule in organic farming for keeping farm animals?
a: The animals always stay in the barn
The animals get antibiotics every day as a precaution
The animals only eat feed from the factory
112349.e: Organic farms must give their animals plenty of space and regular time outdoors. Medicines such as antibiotics are only given when an animal is ill.

112350.q: How do organic farmers usually deal with weeds in the field?
a: Mechanically with a hoe or harrow
112350.e: Instead of spraying herbicides, weeds are removed with hoeing machines, harrows or by hand. This takes more work.
112350.m: In organic farming, weeds are hoed instead of sprayed.

112351.q: What is the aim of organic farming?
a: Keeping the soil fertile and protecting nature
Using as much artificial fertiliser as possible
Creating fields as big as possible without hedges
Growing only plants from the laboratory
112351.e: Organic farmers look after the soil with manure and compost and do without chemical sprays. This is meant to protect the soil, water and animals.
112351.m: Organic farming protects the soil and nature.

112352.q: Why are organic products in the shop often more expensive?
a: Because growing them takes more work and gives smaller harvests
Because they have to come from abroad
112352.e: Without chemical sprays and artificial fertiliser, the harvest is often smaller. Also, things like weed control take more working time.
112352.m: Organic farming takes more work and usually gives smaller harvests.

112353.q: Which symbol does the Bio Suisse label show?
112353.e: The Bio Suisse label is called the “Bud” (Knospe). It is the best-known organic label in Switzerland.
112353.m: The Bud is the symbol of Bio Suisse.

a: The umbrella organisation of Swiss organic farmers
112354.e: Bio Suisse is a private association of Swiss organic producers. It sets rules that are often stricter than the state organic regulations.
112354.m: Bio Suisse is the association of Swiss organic farmers.

112355.q: What does Bio Suisse require of the whole farm?
a: The entire farm must be run organically
Only one field has to be organic
Only the animals have to be organic
Organic rules only apply in summer
112355.e: Bio Suisse follows the whole-farm principle. So a farm may not work partly conventionally and partly organically.
112355.m: With Bio Suisse, the whole farm must be organic.

112356.q: Which type of transport is banned for Bud products from abroad?
112356.e: Bio Suisse bans air freight because it is especially harmful to the climate. So imported Bud products come by ship, train or lorry.
112356.m: Bud products may not be transported by aeroplane.

112357.q: What is banned on farms with the Bio Suisse Bud label?
112357.e: Bud farms may not use synthetic chemical pesticides or artificial fertiliser. They protect their plants with natural methods.
112357.m: Organic farms do without chemical sprays.

112358.q: How long does it take to convert a farm to organic before it gets the full Bud?
112358.e: During the two-year conversion period, the farm already works by organic rules. Its products then carry the conversion Bud.
112358.m: Converting to organic takes two years.

112359.q: What does it mean when the Bud on a packet has a Swiss cross?
a: At least 90 per cent of the ingredients come from Switzerland
112359.e: The Bud with a Swiss cross means that at least 90 per cent of the raw ingredients come from Switzerland. Without the cross, a larger share comes from abroad.
112359.m: The Bud with a Swiss cross stands for Swiss ingredients.

112360.q: Which animal can you see on the IP-Suisse label?
112360.e: The IP-Suisse label shows a ladybird. The beetle stands for controlling pests naturally.
112360.m: You find the ladybird on IP-Suisse products.

112361.q: What does “IP” stand for in IP-Suisse?
112361.e: Integrated production combines modern farming with care for nature. Sprays are only used where needed and as little as possible.

112362.q: What is allowed in integrated production, unlike in organic farming?
112362.e: IP farmers may use synthetic products, but only when needed and in small amounts. In organic farming they are banned.
112362.m: Integrated production lies between conventional and organic.

112363.q: What must IP-Suisse farms especially promote?
112363.e: IP-Suisse farmers collect points for measures such as hedges, flower meadows and piles of stones. This creates habitats for many animals and plants.
112363.m: IP-Suisse farms create habitats for animals and plants.

112364.e: IP-Suisse is an association of farming families who work according to the rules of integrated production. The products are sold through large retailers.
112364.m: IP-Suisse is an association of farming families.

112365.q: What do IP-Suisse farmers do without when growing cereals such as wheat?
112365.e: No insect killers or fungus killers are sprayed on IP-Suisse cereals. This way of growing is called extensive.
112365.m: IP-Suisse cereals grow without insecticides and fungicides.

112366.q: Which label principle applies to animals at IP-Suisse?
a: Especially animal-friendly keeping with outdoor access
Keeping only in a dark barn
112366.e: IP-Suisse requires more space for animals and regular time outdoors. This goes beyond the animal protection law.
112366.m: IP-Suisse requires outdoor access and plenty of space for animals.

112367.q: Which phrase fits integrated production best?
112367.e: Integrated production relies first on preventive and natural measures. Only when these are not enough is there targeted spraying.
112367.m: Integrated production only uses chemicals when necessary.

112368.q: Who pays Swiss farmers direct payments?
112368.e: Every year the federal government gives money to farms. This pays for services that are not covered by the price of food.
112368.m: Direct payments come from the federal government.

112369.q: What do farmers receive direct payments for, for example?
a: For using as much spray as possible
112369.e: Direct payments reward services for the public good, such as landscape care, biodiversity and animal welfare. Food security is supported too.
112369.m: Direct payments reward services for nature and society.

112370.q: What do especially animal-friendly barns under the BTS programme offer the animals?
112370.e: In the BTS programme, the animals live in barns with more space, areas to lie down and daylight. Farmers get extra payments for this.
112370.m: The BTS programme rewards especially animal-friendly barns.

112371.q: Roughly how much money does the federal government pay out in direct payments each year (as of 2024)?
112371.e: Direct payments make up most of the federal government's spending on farming. They come to about 2.8 billion francs a year.
112371.m: The federal government pays billions to farming every year.

112372.q: Which federal office is responsible for direct payments?
112372.e: The Federal Office for Agriculture (FOAG) in Bern carries out agricultural policy. The money is paid to the farms through the cantons.
112372.m: The Federal Office for Agriculture is responsible for agricultural policy.

112373.q: What is the Swiss animal welfare programme “RAUS” about?
112373.e: In the RAUS programme (the name means “out” in German), the animals may regularly go outside to pasture or into an exercise yard. Farmers get extra payments for this.
112373.m: In the RAUS programme, animals regularly go outside.

112374.q: In which document is it laid down that the federal government supports farming?
112374.e: Article 104 of the Federal Constitution describes the tasks of farming. It allows the federal government to pay farmers direct payments for their services.
112374.m: The Federal Constitution requires the federal government to support farming.

112375.q: Why do farmers get extra payments for mowing steep meadows?
a: Because work on a slope takes much more effort
Because no animals may graze there
Because steep meadows belong to the federal government
112375.e: On a steep slope you need special machines and lots of work by hand. Slope payments make up for this extra effort, so that the areas continue to be looked after.
112375.m: Slope payments make up for the hard work on steep meadows.

112377.q: What does Agroscope test before a new cereal variety is recommended in Switzerland?
a: How well it grows here and how healthy it stays
How loudly it rustles in the wind
112377.e: New varieties are tested on trial fields for several years. Only those that give good harvests and rarely get ill are recommended.
112377.m: New varieties are first tested on trial fields.

112378.q: Agroscope also researches bees. Why are bees important for fruit growers?
112378.e: Without pollination, apple or cherry trees produce hardly any fruit. Bees carry pollen from flower to flower.

112379.q: What is a particular aim of plant breeding at Agroscope?
a: Plants that only grow in winter
112379.e: Resistant varieties get ill less often. So you can save on sprays and still have a good harvest.

112380.q: What does Agroscope provide for cheese dairies?
112380.e: Agroscope breeds and supplies lactic acid bacteria that dairies need for Emmental, Gruyère and other cheeses. These cultures shape the flavour and the holes.
112380.m: Agroscope's bacterial cultures help with cheesemaking.

112381.q: Who owns the Agroscope research centre?
112381.e: Agroscope is part of the federal administration. It belongs to the Federal Office for Agriculture.
112381.m: Agroscope is the federal government's agricultural research.

112382.q: What are Agroscope's trial fields for?
a: To test plants under real conditions
112382.e: On trial fields, researchers compare varieties, fertilisers and growing methods. This shows them what really works outdoors.
112382.m: Farming is tested outdoors on trial fields.

112383.q: Which insect, brought in from North America, destroyed many vines in Europe in the 19th century?
112383.e: Phylloxera damages the roots of European vines. Since then, vines have been grafted onto resistant American rootstocks.
112383.m: Phylloxera almost destroyed winegrowing in Europe.

112384.q: Which substance in grape juice turns into alcohol during fermentation?
112384.e: Yeasts feed on the sugar in grape juice. This produces alcohol and carbon dioxide, and so juice becomes wine.
112384.m: During fermentation, sugar turns into alcohol.

112385.q: Why do vines grow especially well in Ticino?
a: The climate south of the Alps is mild and sunny
The ground there is always frozen
112385.e: Ticino lies south of the Alps. It has lots of sun and mild temperatures, ideal for vines that like warmth.
112385.m: Vines grow very well in mild Ticino.

112386.q: In which season are grapes harvested in Switzerland?
112386.e: The grapes ripen all summer. They are usually harvested in September and October.
112386.m: The grape harvest takes place in autumn.

112387.q: What is young, still fermenting grape juice called in Switzerland in autumn?
112387.e: Sauser is grape juice that has just started to ferment. It tastes sweet, is slightly fizzy and already contains a little alcohol.
112387.m: Sauser is fermenting grape juice from the autumn.

112388.q: Why are vineyards often planted on south-facing slopes?
a: The vines get the most sun there
There is the most shade there
112388.e: A south-facing slope gets sunshine almost all day. This makes the grapes sweet and ripe.

112389.q: Why do fruit growers prune their trees in winter?
a: So that more light gets into the crown
So that the trees die faster
So that the bees stay away
So that the leaves fall earlier
112389.e: In winter pruning, old branches and branches that are too dense are removed. So the fruit gets more light and grows bigger and healthier.
112389.m: Winter pruning lets light into the tree's crown.

112390.q: Which fruit is grown most in Switzerland?
112390.e: Apples are Switzerland's most important fruit. They store well and can be sold all year round.
112390.m: The apple is number one in Swiss fruit growing.

112391.q: What is it called when fruit growers remove some of the young fruit from the tree?
112391.e: If a tree has too many fruits, they stay small and the tree often bears less the next year. That is why surplus young fruits are removed when thinning.
112391.m: Thinning makes the remaining fruit bigger.

112392.q: Why are apples stored in cool stores with little oxygen?
a: So that they stay fresh for months
112392.e: Cold and low oxygen slow down the apples' breathing. So they ripen more slowly and can be sold until the next harvest.
112392.m: Cool stores keep apples fresh until the next harvest.

112393.q: Which animals are especially important for pollinating fruit blossom?
112393.e: Bees carry pollen from flower to flower. Without pollination, hardly any fruit would form on the trees.
112393.m: Without bees there would be much less fruit.

112394.q: Which dangerous bacterial disease attacks apple and pear trees?
112394.e: With fire blight, leaves and shoots look as if they have been burnt. Sick trees often have to be cut down so that the disease does not spread.
112394.m: Fire blight is a dangerous disease of apple and pear trees.

112395.q: Why do fruit growers stretch nets over their trees?
a: So that the trees grow faster
So that bees cannot get in
112395.e: Hailstones damage the fruit and make it impossible to sell. Hail nets catch the hailstones.
112395.m: Hail nets protect fruit from hail damage.

112396.q: What are the modern orchards with many small, low apple trees in long rows called?
112396.e: In low-stem orchards, many small trees stand close together in rows. They can be looked after and harvested without long ladders, and they bear fruit after just a few years.
112396.m: Most eating apples today grow in low-stem orchards.

112397.q: Which fruit is the region around Zug traditionally known for?
112397.e: Lots of cherry trees have grown around Zug for a long time. Apricots, on the other hand, are typical of Valais, and oranges and bananas grow in warm countries.
112397.m: Zug is known for its cherries.

112398.q: What is it called when rain washes unprotected field soil down a slope?
112398.e: If a field lies without a plant cover, heavy rain can wash away fertile soil. Catch crops and mulch protect the soil from this.
112398.m: Plants protect field soil from erosion.

112399.q: What does Bio Suisse require when keeping farm animals?
a: Keeping only in a dark barn
As many animals as possible in a small space
112399.e: Bud animals must regularly go outside and get mainly feed from Switzerland. This lets them move in a way that suits their species.

112401.q: Which eye problem often occurs with a pollen allergy?
112401.e: Pollen lands on the conjunctiva of the eyes. In people with allergies it becomes inflamed, and the eyes turn red, itch and water.
112401.m: With a pollen allergy, the conjunctiva of the eyes often becomes inflamed.

112402.q: Why is a close-fitting pair of sunglasses useful for people with a pollen allergy when cycling?
a: They keep pollen away from the eyes
They filter pollen out of the air you breathe
112402.e: When cycling, lots of pollen flies straight into your face. Close-fitting glasses keep some of it away from the sensitive eyes.
112402.m: Glasses protect the eyes of people with pollen allergies from pollen.

112403.q: What do you call a substance that triggers an allergy?
112403.e: An allergen is a substance, usually containing protein, that the immune system reacts to allergically, for example a pollen grain or a food.
112403.m: A substance that triggers an allergy is called an allergen.

112404.q: Which symptoms are typical of a pollen allergy?
a: Sneezing, a runny nose and itchy eyes
112404.e: Pollen mainly irritates the mucous membranes of the nose and eyes. That is why sufferers often sneeze, have a runny nose and itchy, watery eyes.
112404.m: Hay fever mainly shows up in the nose and eyes.

112405.q: Why do plants with large, colourful flowers such as roses rarely cause hay fever?
a: Their pollen is carried by insects, not by the wind
Their pollen is smaller than dust
They produce no pollen at all
112405.e: Insect-pollinated plants have heavy, sticky pollen that hardly gets into the air. Hay fever is mainly caused by wind-pollinated plants such as grasses and many trees.
112405.m: Hay fever mainly comes from wind-pollinated plants.

112406.q: How can a pollen allergy be weakened in a targeted way over several years?
a: With regular small amounts of the allergen
With lots of sport when pollen counts are high
112406.e: In this treatment you receive small amounts of the allergen over several years. The immune system gets used to it and reacts less strongly.
112406.m: Small amounts of the allergen can get the body used to pollen.

112407.q: What can happen if hay fever is not treated for years?
a: The allergy can spread to the lungs and cause asthma
112407.e: Without treatment, the symptoms can move from the nose into the bronchial tubes. Allergic asthma can develop.
112407.m: Untreated hay fever can lead to asthma.

112408.q: Roughly what share of the Swiss population suffers from a pollen allergy?
112408.e: According to the Swiss Allergy Centre (aha!), around 20 per cent of the population suffer from a pollen allergy. This makes it one of the most common allergies.
112408.m: About one person in five in Switzerland has a pollen allergy.

112409.q: Which group of animals do house dust mites belong to?
112409.e: Like spiders, mites have eight legs, so they belong to the arachnids. Insects, on the other hand, have six legs.
112409.m: House dust mites are tiny arachnids with eight legs.

112410.q: What do house dust mites mainly feed on?
112410.e: People lose tiny flakes of skin every day. House dust mites live on these, especially where we spend a lot of time.
112410.m: House dust mites eat our flakes of skin.

112411.q: What mainly causes the symptoms of a house dust mite allergy?
112411.e: The allergens are mainly found in the mites’ tiny droppings. These break down into fine dust, which is breathed in.
112411.m: With a mite allergy, you mainly react to mite droppings.

112412.q: Where in a home do particularly large numbers of house dust mites live?
112412.e: In bed, mites find warmth, moisture from sweating and lots of skin flakes. That is why so many live there.
112412.m: Most house dust mites live in the bed.

112413.q: Which indoor climate do house dust mites particularly like?
112413.e: Mites thrive at room temperature and high humidity. They take in moisture directly from the air.
112413.m: House dust mites love warm, humid air.

112414.q: Why is a vacuum cleaner with a HEPA filter useful for people with a mite allergy?
a: It kills the mites with electricity
It makes the air more humid
112414.e: Ordinary vacuum cleaners blow some fine mite droppings back into the air. A HEPA filter traps even very small particles.
112414.m: A HEPA filter stops allergens being stirred up when vacuuming.

112415.q: When are the symptoms of a house dust mite allergy usually at their worst?
a: At night and in the morning after getting up
Only in spring when it is sunny
112415.e: In bed you breathe in mite allergens for hours. That is why a blocked nose and sneezing are usually worst at night and in the morning.
112415.m: A mite allergy is especially troublesome at night and in the morning.

112416.q: Which measure helps with a house dust mite allergy?
a: Mite-proof covers for the mattress and pillow
Lots of cuddly toys in bed
112416.e: Special mite-proof covers (encasings) keep the allergens inside the mattress. It also helps to wash bedding at a high temperature and air the room well.
112416.m: Mite-proof covers protect against mite allergens in bed.

112417.q: Can you see house dust mites with the naked eye?
a: Yes, they are as big as ants
Yes, they are as big as ladybirds
Yes, they are as big as houseflies
112417.e: House dust mites are usually only about a third of a millimetre long. You can only see them under a microscope or a strong magnifying glass.
112417.m: House dust mites cannot be seen with the naked eye.

112418.q: How must peanuts appear in the ingredients list of a food in Switzerland?
a: Not at all if there is only a little
112418.e: Peanuts are one of the main allergens. These must be clearly highlighted in the ingredients list, for example in bold, so that people with allergies can find them quickly.
112418.m: Main allergens such as peanuts are highlighted in the ingredients list.

112419.q: Which treatment can reduce some children’s sensitivity to peanuts under medical supervision?
a: Tiny, slowly increasing amounts of peanut protein
112419.e: In oral immunotherapy, the child receives a tiny amount of peanut protein every day, which is slowly increased. This may only be done under medical supervision, because reactions are possible.
112419.m: A peanut allergy may only be treated under medical supervision.

112420.q: What does the label “May contain traces of peanuts” on a packet mean?
a: Small amounts may get in during production
The product has been tested as peanut-free
112420.e: Peanuts are not an ingredient, but they are processed in the same factory. For people with a strong allergy, even this small amount can be dangerous.
112420.m: A traces warning warns of small, unintended amounts of an allergen.

112421.q: Why is a peanut allergy particularly feared?
a: Even tiny amounts can cause severe reactions
It only causes a mild skin rash
It only occurs in older people
It is contagious from person to person
112421.e: With a peanut allergy, even traces can trigger a life-threatening reaction. It is one of the most common causes of serious food allergy emergencies.
112421.m: With a peanut allergy, even traces can be dangerous.

112422.q: Does a peanut allergy usually go away by itself over time?
a: No, for most people it lasts a lifetime
Yes, almost always by the time children start school
Yes, if you eat peanuts every day
112422.e: Only a small number of children grow out of a peanut allergy. For most people affected, it lasts a lifetime.
112422.m: A peanut allergy usually lasts for life.

112423.q: Which group of plants does the peanut actually belong to?
112423.e: The peanut is not a real nut but a legume, like peas and beans. Its fruits ripen in the ground.

112424.q: Which dish particularly often contains peanuts?
112424.e: Satay sauce is made from ground peanuts. Peanuts can also be hidden in Asian dishes and muesli bars.

112425.q: Which protein from cereals triggers coeliac disease?
112425.e: In coeliac disease, the body cannot tolerate the cereal protein gluten. Casein, on the other hand, comes from milk, albumin from egg white and keratin from hair and nails.
112425.m: Coeliac disease is triggered by gluten.

112426.e: Gluten is found in wheat, rye and barley, for example. Rice, maize and millet are naturally gluten-free.

112427.q: Which organ is mainly damaged by coeliac disease?
112427.e: In coeliac disease, gluten makes the lining of the small intestine inflamed. As a result, the body absorbs nutrients less well.
112427.m: Coeliac disease damages the small intestine.

112428.q: Which cereal must people with coeliac disease also avoid?
112428.e: Spelt is closely related to wheat and also contains gluten. Despite its name, buckwheat is not wheat and is gluten-free.

a: With an operation on the intestine
112429.e: There is no medicine that cures coeliac disease. People who stick strictly to a gluten-free diet usually have no more symptoms, and the intestine recovers.
112429.m: With coeliac disease you must eat gluten-free all your life.

112430.q: Which side dish is naturally gluten-free?
112430.e: Potatoes contain no gluten. Spaghetti, couscous and bulgur, on the other hand, are made from wheat.

112431.q: Which symbol often marks gluten-free foods?
112431.e: The crossed-out ear of grain shows that a product is gluten-free. It helps people with coeliac disease when shopping.
112431.m: The crossed-out ear of grain means gluten-free.

112432.q: What happens in the body of someone with coeliac disease when they eat gluten?
a: The body’s defences attack the lining of the intestine
The body suddenly lacks vitamin C
112432.e: In coeliac disease, the body’s defences react wrongly to gluten and turn against the body’s own intestinal lining. So coeliac disease is not an infection and not poisoning.
112432.m: In coeliac disease, the body’s defences attack the intestine because of gluten.

112433.q: Roughly how many people have coeliac disease?
112433.e: Estimates suggest that around one per cent of the population have coeliac disease. Many do not know it, because the symptoms vary a great deal.
112433.m: About one per cent of people have coeliac disease.

a: A reaction to similar proteins in different substances
An allergy to plants with cross-shaped flowers
An allergy that only lasts two days
112434.e: In a cross-allergy, the immune system reacts to another substance because its proteins resemble the original allergen. This way, a pollen allergy can also cause reactions to foods.
112434.m: In a cross-allergy, the immune system confuses similar proteins.

112435.q: Which fruit do people with a birch pollen allergy particularly often react to?
112435.e: A protein in apples is very similar to the main allergen in birch pollen. That is why many people with a birch pollen allergy feel a tingling in the mouth when eating raw apples.
112435.m: People with a birch pollen allergy often cannot tolerate raw apples well.

112436.q: Which nut often causes a cross-reaction in people with a birch pollen allergy?
112436.e: Hazel and birch are closely related, and their proteins are similar. That is why people with a birch pollen allergy often also react to hazelnuts.
112436.m: The hazelnut is a cross-allergen that goes with birch.

112437.q: Which symptom is typical when people with a pollen allergy eat a cross-reacting fruit?
a: Tingling and itching in the mouth
Hair loss at the back of the head
112437.e: In what is called oral allergy syndrome, the lips, tongue and palate itch or tingle shortly after eating. Sometimes the lining of the mouth swells slightly.
112437.m: Cross-allergies to fruit often show up as itching in the mouth.

112438.q: Why can many people with a birch pollen allergy eat cooked apple purée but not a raw apple?
a: The protein causing the reaction is destroyed by heat
112438.e: The apple allergen that resembles the birch pollen allergen is sensitive to heat. When cooked or baked, it changes shape and the immune system no longer recognises it.
112438.m: Heat makes many fruit allergens harmless.

112439.q: Which fruit do people with a latex allergy often react to as well?
112439.e: In latex-fruit syndrome, people allergic to latex also react to fruits such as banana, avocado or kiwi. The reason is similar proteins.
112439.m: A latex allergy can be linked to a banana allergy.

112440.q: Which vegetable often causes a cross-reaction in people with a mugwort pollen allergy?
112440.e: Mugwort and celery have similar proteins. This is called celery-mugwort-spice syndrome, because spices can also be affected.
112440.m: Mugwort pollen and celery are a typical cross-allergy pair.

112441.q: Which foods can people with a house dust mite allergy react to because of a cross-allergy?
112441.e: Mites and crustaceans are both arthropods and have a similar muscle protein called tropomyosin. That is why cross-reactions are possible.
112441.m: A mite allergy and a crustacean allergy can be linked.

112442.q: Why should fresh fish always be kept well chilled?
a: Otherwise bacteria produce harmful substances such as histamine
Otherwise it becomes too hard to fry
112442.e: When it is warm, bacteria multiply in the fish. In doing so they produce histamine, which can cause flushing, headaches and nausea after eating.
112442.m: Poorly chilled fish can contain a lot of histamine.

112443.q: When does the body release a particularly large amount of histamine?
112443.e: When the immune system recognises an allergy trigger such as pollen, certain cells suddenly release histamine. This leads to sneezing, itching and swelling.
112443.m: In allergies, the body releases a lot of histamine.

112444.q: What effect does released histamine have in the skin?
112444.e: Histamine widens the blood vessels and makes them leakier. The skin turns red, swells and itches, as after a mosquito bite.
112444.m: Histamine makes the skin itch and swell.

112445.q: What are medicines that block the effect of histamine called?
112445.e: Antihistamines occupy the docking sites for histamine. In this way they relieve sneezing, itching and watery eyes.
112445.m: Antihistamines block the effect of histamine.

112446.q: Why do older allergy medicines against histamine often make you tired?
a: Histamine keeps you awake in the brain
They contain a lot of alcohol
112446.e: In the brain, histamine acts as a messenger for wakefulness. Older medicines reach the brain and block this effect there; newer ones hardly do.
112446.m: In the brain, histamine keeps you awake.

112447.q: From which amino acid does the body make histamine?
112447.e: Histamine is made from the amino acid histidine by removing a small chemical group. That is why the names of the two substances are almost the same.
112447.m: Histamine is made from the amino acid histidine.

112448.q: Which food contains a particularly large amount of histamine?
112448.e: During long maturing, microorganisms produce histamine. People with histamine intolerance therefore often do not tolerate matured cheese well.
112448.m: Long-matured foods contain a lot of histamine.

112449.q: What is it called when someone does not tolerate histamine from food well?
112449.e: With histamine intolerance, the intestine breaks down too little histamine from food. After cheese, wine or sauerkraut, symptoms can then occur.
112449.m: Someone who tolerates histamine poorly has histamine intolerance.

112450.q: Which fermented vegetable is particularly rich in histamine?
112450.e: Sauerkraut is made by fermentation with lactic acid bacteria. This produces a lot of histamine, whereas fresh vegetables contain hardly any.
112450.m: Sauerkraut contains a lot of histamine because of fermentation.

112451.q: What most often triggers anaphylaxis in children?
112451.e: In children, foods such as peanuts, nuts, milk and egg are the most common triggers. In adults, insect stings and medicines play a bigger role.
112451.m: In children, anaphylaxis is usually triggered by foods.

112452.q: Which existing illness makes anaphylaxis particularly dangerous?
112452.e: With asthma, the airways are already sensitive. If they also swell up during anaphylaxis, severe breathing difficulties can quickly follow.
112452.m: Asthma increases the risk of severe anaphylaxis.

112453.q: What happens to blood pressure during anaphylactic shock?
112453.e: Many messenger substances such as histamine suddenly widen the blood vessels. As a result, blood pressure falls and organs get too little blood.
112453.m: During anaphylaxis, blood pressure drops dangerously.

112454.q: Which sign points to dangerous anaphylaxis?
112454.e: If the throat or airways swell, the person cannot breathe properly. This is a warning sign of a severe allergic reaction.
112454.m: Breathlessness after contact with an allergen is a warning sign.

112455.q: How quickly does anaphylaxis usually develop?
112455.e: Anaphylaxis usually begins a few minutes to about an hour after contact with the allergen. That is why you must act quickly.

112456.q: How should you position a person with anaphylaxis who mainly has circulation problems but is breathing well?
a: Lying flat with the legs raised
Lying on their front with the head down
112456.e: With circulation problems, raising the legs helps more blood flow to the heart and brain. If the person is short of breath, however, let them sit upright.
112456.m: With circulation problems, raise the legs.

112457.q: Why must you go to hospital after anaphylaxis, even if you are already feeling better?
a: The reaction can come back hours later
Only there can you collect your emergency card
The health insurer requires a report
There you are immediately vaccinated against the allergy
112457.e: After anaphylaxis, a second wave of reaction can follow, even if you feel better at first. That is why you are monitored in hospital for a few hours.
112457.m: After anaphylaxis, you belong in hospital for monitoring.

112458.q: Which skin signs often appear during anaphylaxis?
a: Itchy weals like after stinging nettles
112458.e: Itchy, raised weals often appear all over the body. They are often the first visible sign.
112458.m: Weals all over the body can signal anaphylaxis.

112459.q: Where do you inject an adrenaline auto-injector in an emergency?
a: Into the outer side of the thigh
Into the tummy next to the belly button
Into the inner side of the upper arm
Into the palm of the hand
112459.e: The large muscle on the outer side of the thigh absorbs the adrenaline quickly. You press the injector firmly there until it fires.
112459.m: You place the adrenaline auto-injector on the outer thigh.

112460.q: Can you inject an adrenaline auto-injector through trousers?
a: Yes, that is allowed in an emergency
No, the skin must be disinfected first
112460.e: The needle goes through normal clothing. That way no time is lost undressing in an emergency.
112460.m: An adrenaline auto-injector can be used through clothing.

112461.q: What does adrenaline do during a severe allergic reaction?
a: It makes breathing easier and supports the circulation
It makes you tired and sleepy
It makes blood pressure drop further
It cures the allergy for ever
112461.e: Adrenaline widens the airways and raises the dangerously low blood pressure again. But the allergy itself does not go away.
112461.m: Adrenaline supports the circulation and opens the airways.

112462.q: What should a child with a severe allergy always have with them?
a: Their emergency kit with the adrenaline auto-injector
112462.e: In a severe allergic reaction, every minute counts. That is why people with allergies always carry their emergency kit with the adrenaline auto-injector.
112462.m: People with allergies always carry their emergency kit.

112463.q: What do you do if the liquid in the viewing window of an adrenaline auto-injector is discoloured or cloudy?
a: Warm it up in the oven
112463.e: Normally the adrenaline solution is clear and colourless. If it is brownish or cloudy, the active ingredient has broken down and the device must be replaced.
112463.m: A discoloured adrenaline solution must be replaced.

112464.q: What must you check regularly on an adrenaline auto-injector?
112464.e: Adrenaline only keeps for a limited time. An expired auto-injector may work less well and should be replaced.
112464.m: Check the expiry date of the emergency kit regularly.

112465.q: How should you store an adrenaline auto-injector correctly?
a: In a hot car in the sun
112465.e: Adrenaline is sensitive to heat and cold. Store the auto-injector at room temperature and always carry it with you.
112465.m: The adrenaline auto-injector must not be kept in heat or cold.

112466.q: What determines which dose an adrenaline auto-injector contains?
112466.e: For smaller children, there are auto-injectors with less adrenaline than for adults. The doctor chooses the dose according to body weight.
112466.m: The adrenaline dose depends on body weight.

112467.q: When should you use the adrenaline auto-injector if there are signs of a severe allergy?
a: Only once the person is unconscious
Only after phoning the family doctor
112467.e: Adrenaline works best when it is given early. Waiting too long is more dangerous than an injection that later turns out to have been unnecessary.
112467.m: In a severe allergic reaction, give adrenaline early.

112468.q: What is a classic measuring device called that draws in air and collects the pollen in it on a sticky strip?
112468.e: The pollen trap draws in air continuously, and the pollen sticks to a sticky strip. Experts then identify and count it under the microscope.
112468.m: A pollen trap measures how much pollen is in the air.

112469.q: In which months does grass pollen mainly fly in Switzerland?
112469.e: Grasses mainly flower in late spring and early summer. Most people with pollen allergies suffer most at this time.
112469.m: Grass pollen mainly flies in early summer.

112470.q: Which introduced plant causes strong pollen allergies in late summer and should be controlled?
112470.e: Ragweed comes from North America and flowers from about August to October. Its pollen is highly allergenic, which is why it is strictly controlled in Switzerland.
112470.m: The introduced ragweed is a strong allergy trigger.

112471.q: How does prolonged rain affect the amount of pollen in the air?
a: It washes the pollen out of the air
It doubles the amount of pollen
112471.e: Rain binds the pollen and brings it to the ground. After heavy rain, the air therefore often contains much less pollen.
112471.m: Rain cleans pollen out of the air.

112472.q: Why is the pollen load usually lower in the mountains?
a: Fewer plants flower there, and later
112472.e: At higher altitudes, plants are sparser and flowering starts later. That is why many people with allergies feel better in the mountains.
112472.m: In the mountains, the pollen load is usually lower.

112473.q: Why can the start of a thunderstorm be particularly unpleasant for people with a pollen allergy?
a: Pollen grains burst and break into tiny particles
The thunder irritates the lining of the nose
The pollen becomes bigger and heavier
112473.e: Moisture makes pollen grains burst, and strong gusts of wind spread the tiny fragments. These get deep into the airways and can trigger asthma attacks; this is called thunderstorm asthma.
112473.m: At the start of a thunderstorm, burst pollen can trigger asthma.

112474.q: In which unit is the pollen concentration in the air given?
a: Pollen per cubic metre of air
112474.e: The pollen concentration tells you how many pollen grains are floating in one cubic metre of air. The higher the value, the more people with allergies suffer.
112474.m: Pollen concentration is measured in pollen per cubic metre of air.

112475.q: How is climate change altering the pollen season in Switzerland?
a: It starts earlier and lasts longer
It starts later and is shorter
In some years it does not happen at all
It only takes place in winter
112475.e: Warmer temperatures make many plants flower earlier. Measurements by MeteoSwiss show that the pollen season starts earlier for several species.
112475.m: Because of global warming, the pollen season starts earlier.

112476.q: Which insects most often cause an insect venom allergy in Switzerland?
112476.e: Bees and wasps inject venom when they sting. Some people react allergically to it, up to life-threatening shock.
112476.m: Bees and wasps are the main causes of insect venom allergies.

112477.q: What usually happens to a honeybee after it has stung a person?
a: It sleeps for a whole day
It immediately grows a new sting
112477.e: The honeybee’s sting has barbs and stays stuck in the skin. When the bee flies away, the sting tears off together with the venom sac, and the bee dies.
112477.m: A honeybee usually dies after stinging the skin.

112478.q: Why can a wasp sting several times in a row?
a: Its sting is smooth and does not get stuck
It carries a lot of venom in its head
112478.e: The wasp’s sting has hardly any barbs. So the wasp can pull it out again and sting again.

112479.q: Is the saying true that a few hornet stings can kill a horse?
a: No, a hornet sting is hardly more dangerous than a wasp sting
112479.e: A hornet’s venom is no stronger per sting than a wasp’s. A sting is mainly dangerous with an allergy or with a very large number of stings.
112479.m: For healthy people, a hornet sting is no more dangerous than a wasp sting.

112480.q: Why is a wasp sting in the mouth dangerous even without an allergy?
a: The swelling can narrow the airways
The venom goes straight to the brain
You lose your sense of taste
112480.e: If the tongue or throat swells badly, it can become hard to breathe. That is why a sting in the mouth or throat must always be taken seriously.
112480.m: A sting in the mouth can be dangerous because of the swelling.

112481.q: What helps as a first measure after an insect sting in the mouth?
a: Sucking ice or drinking something cold
112481.e: Cold slows down the swelling in the mouth and throat. At the same time, if there are breathing problems, you should call the emergency number at once.
112481.m: After a sting in the mouth, cold helps against the swelling.

112482.q: In which season are wasps particularly common and pushy?
112482.e: In late summer, wasp colonies are at their largest. The insects then search more for sweet food, drinks and meat.
112482.m: In late summer there are particularly many wasps.

112483.q: Why should people with a bee venom allergy not walk barefoot across flowering meadows in summer?
a: They might step on a bee
The grass is particularly sharp then
Pollen gets in through the sole of the foot
112483.e: Bees collect nectar from clover and other low flowers. If you step on one barefoot, the bee stings to defend itself.
112483.m: Walking barefoot across flower meadows can lead to bee stings.

112484.q: What is the most common skin test for detecting allergies such as hay fever called?
112484.e: In the skin prick test, the skin is pricked lightly through drops containing allergens. If you are allergic, a skin reaction appears after a short time.
112484.m: The skin prick test is the most important skin test for allergies.

112485.q: On which part of the body is a skin prick test usually done?
a: On the inside of the forearm
On the sole of the foot
112485.e: The inside of the forearm is easy to reach and the skin there is thin. Sometimes the test is also done on the back.
112485.m: The skin prick test is usually done on the forearm.

112486.q: After how long is a skin prick test read?
112486.e: Immediate-type allergies show up quickly. After about a quarter of an hour, the specialist measures the size of the skin reaction.
112486.m: A skin prick test is read after about a quarter of an hour.

112487.q: How can you recognise a positive reaction in a skin prick test?
112487.e: With an allergy, a raised, itchy weal with a red ring forms at the test site. The bigger it is, the stronger the sensitisation.
112487.m: An itchy weal in a skin prick test indicates an allergy.

112488.q: Why are several substances tested at the same time in a skin prick test?
a: To find out which substance you are allergic to
So that you get better faster
So that the skin itches less
So that blood can be taken at the same time
112488.e: Drops with different allergens, such as pollen, animal hair or mites, are placed on the forearm. The spot where a weal appears shows the trigger.
112488.m: The skin prick test shows which substances you are allergic to.

112489.q: Why does the skin itch during an allergic reaction in a skin prick test?
a: The body releases the substance histamine
The light in the room irritates the skin
112489.e: In an allergy, immune cells release histamine. It makes the skin red, causes a weal and triggers itching.
112489.m: In allergies, histamine causes redness and itching.

112490.q: Which medicines must you stop taking for a few days before a skin prick test?
112490.e: Medicines against histamine suppress the skin reaction. The test could then wrongly come out negative.
112490.m: Before a skin test, stop allergy medicines after talking to the doctor.

112491.q: Why is a patch test for contact allergies such as nickel only read after two to three days?
a: Contact allergies only show up after a delay
The patch has to dry first
The doctor has no time before then
The nickel has to rust first
112491.e: With contact allergies, the skin does not react straight away but only after hours or days. That is why the test patches stay on the back for longer.
112491.m: Contact allergies only show up after some time.

112492.q: Which examination can add to or replace a skin test for allergies?
112492.e: Special antibodies against individual allergens can be measured in the blood. This is useful when a skin test is not possible, for example with a severe skin rash.
112492.m: Allergies can also be detected with a blood test.

112493.q: Which foods most often cause allergies in young children?
112493.e: Cow’s milk and hen’s eggs are among the most common allergy triggers in babies and young children. Rice and many vegetables, on the other hand, are rarely a problem.
112493.m: In young children, milk and egg are common allergy triggers.

112494.q: What is the body missing in lactose intolerance?
112494.e: Without lactase, milk sugar cannot be broken down in the intestine. This leads to tummy ache and wind, but it is not an allergy, because the immune system is not involved.
112494.m: In lactose intolerance, the enzyme lactase is missing.

112495.q: What must be stated on packaged foods in Switzerland so that people with allergies can shop safely?
a: The main allergens they contain, such as milk or nuts
The weight of every single ingredient
112495.e: Main allergens such as cereals containing gluten, milk, eggs, peanuts or celery must be declared on the packaging.
112495.m: Main allergens must be stated on foods.

112496.q: Do restaurants in Switzerland have to give information about allergens in their dishes?
a: Yes, they must provide information when asked
112496.e: Even with food sold unpackaged, guests must be able to find out which main allergens it contains. The staff must be able to give this information.
112496.m: Restaurants must give information about allergens.

112497.q: Which body system overreacts in a food allergy?
112497.e: In an allergy, the immune system mistakes a harmless substance from food for a dangerous one and fights it fiercely.
112497.m: In an allergy, the immune system overreacts.

112498.q: What happens to many children with a milk or egg allergy over the years?
a: It turns into a pollen allergy
112498.e: Many children develop a tolerance to milk and egg over time. Whether this is the case is checked by a doctor.
112498.m: Milk and egg allergies go away in many children.

112499.q: What is the most important measure for a food allergy?
112499.e: For most food allergies, there is no cure yet. That is why the most important thing is not to eat the food that causes it.
112499.m: With a food allergy, you avoid the allergen.

112500.q: Which seeds are among the main allergens that must be declared?
112500.e: Sesame is one of the main allergens that must be declared and stated on foods. It is found, for example, in bread rolls, hummus or sesame oil.
112500.m: Sesame is a main allergen that must be declared.

112501.q: What is a problem with freshly harvested cassava roots?
a: They go bad after just a few days
112501.e: Harvested cassava roots often become spotty and inedible after just one to three days. That is why they are processed quickly, for example into flour or dried pieces.
112501.m: Freshly harvested cassava must be processed quickly because it spoils fast.

112502.q: Which continent does cassava originally come from?
112502.e: Cassava was first grown in the Amazon region of South America. Portuguese sailors later brought it to Africa and Asia.
112502.m: Cassava originally comes from South America.

112503.q: Why must you not eat cassava raw?
a: It contains far too much sugar
It is full of hard stones
112503.e: Cassava contains substances that can turn into poisonous hydrogen cyanide. Peeling, soaking, boiling or roasting removes the poison.
112503.m: Cassava must be well prepared and cooked before eating because it contains poisonous substances.

112504.q: What is the starch from cassava called, which is used for example to make the little balls in bubble tea?
112504.e: Tapioca is almost pure starch taken from cassava roots. It is used for pearls, puddings and to thicken food.
112504.m: Tapioca is a starch made from cassava.

112505.q: What other name is cassava also known by?
112505.e: Cassava is also called manioc, or yuca in Latin America. Okra, Jerusalem artichoke and parsnip are completely different vegetables.
112505.m: In many countries cassava is also called manioc.

112506.q: On which continent is most cassava grown today?
112506.e: Cassava comes from South America, but today it is grown mainly in Africa. In many African countries it is a staple food.
112506.m: Today most cassava is grown in Africa.

112507.q: How is cassava usually propagated in farming?
112507.e: Farmers push pieces of the woody stem into the ground, and new plants grow from them. Seeds are used almost only in plant breeding.
112507.m: Cassava is usually grown from pieces of stem.

112508.q: Which plant family does cassava belong to?
112508.e: Cassava (Manihot esculenta) belongs to the spurge family. The poinsettia also belongs to this family.
112508.m: Cassava belongs to the spurge family.

112509.q: Why is cassava such an important food in many tropical countries?
a: It grows even on poor soil and in drought
It only grows in cool mountain regions
It needs artificial watering every day
It can only be grown in a greenhouse
112509.e: Cassava is very undemanding and survives even long dry periods. The roots can also stay in the ground for a long time until they are needed.
112509.m: Cassava is important because it grows even on poor soil and in drought.

112510.q: Which group of plants does the soya bean belong to?
112510.e: The soya bean forms pods, usually with two to three seeds. This makes it related to peas, lentils and beans.
112510.m: Like peas and lentils, the soya bean is a legume.

112511.q: Which region of the world does the soya bean originally come from?
112511.e: The soya bean was bred from a wild plant in China thousands of years ago. From East Asia it spread around the world.
112511.m: The soya bean originally comes from East Asia.

112512.q: What is the Japanese seasoning paste made from fermented soya beans, used to make a well-known soup?
112512.e: For miso, soya beans are fermented for months with salt and a special mould (koji). It is used, among other things, to make miso soup.
112512.m: Miso is a seasoning paste made from fermented soya beans.

112513.q: Which two countries harvest the most soya beans (as of 2023)?
112513.e: Together, Brazil and the USA produce well over half of the world's soya harvest. China, on the other hand, is the biggest buyer of soya beans.
112513.m: Brazil and the USA are the world's biggest soya producers.

112514.q: After palm oil, which vegetable oil is produced most worldwide?
112514.e: Pressing soya beans produces soya oil, and the rest is made into feed. Only palm oil is produced in even larger amounts.
112514.m: After palm oil, soya oil is the most produced vegetable oil in the world.

112515.q: What are green soya beans harvested before they are ripe and eaten cooked as a snack called?
112515.e: Edamame are young soya beans that are boiled in their pods and lightly salted. The name comes from Japanese.
112515.m: Edamame are unripe, cooked soya beans.

112516.q: Which nutrient makes the soya bean especially valuable for a vegetarian diet?
112516.e: Dried soya beans are about one third protein. This makes them one of the plants richest in protein.
112516.m: Soya beans are a very good plant source of protein.

112517.q: In which country is the original home of Arabica coffee?
112517.e: Arabica coffee grows wild in the mountain forests of Ethiopia. It reached the Arab world via Yemen and later Europe.
112517.m: Arabica coffee originally comes from Ethiopia.

112518.q: Which two kinds of coffee are the most important in the world?
112518.e: Arabica (Coffea arabica) and Robusta (Coffea canephora) make up almost all of the world's coffee trade. Robusta contains more caffeine and tastes more bitter.
112518.m: The most important kinds of coffee are Arabica and Robusta.

112519.q: What are the fruits of the coffee plant called?
112519.e: The ripe fruits are red and look like small cherries. The coffee beans are inside them.
112519.m: The fruits of the coffee plant are called coffee cherries.

112520.q: How many seeds (beans) does a coffee cherry normally contain?
112520.e: A coffee cherry usually contains two seeds lying with their flat sides together. Occasionally there is just one round bean, called a peaberry.
112520.m: A coffee cherry usually contains two coffee beans.

112521.q: Which country has long been the world's biggest coffee producer?
112521.e: For more than 150 years, Brazil has harvested more coffee than any other country. About a third of the world's coffee comes from there.
112521.m: Brazil produces more coffee than any other country.

112522.q: Which country in South-East Asia is the second-biggest coffee producer and mainly grows Robusta?
112522.e: Vietnam has greatly expanded coffee growing since the 1980s. Mainly Robusta coffee is harvested there.
112522.m: Vietnam is the world's second-biggest coffee producer.

112523.q: Why is the “coffee bean” not really a bean at all?
a: It is the seed of a coffee cherry
112523.e: Coffee beans are the seeds from the red fruit of the coffee plant. The coffee plant is not related to real beans and peas.
112523.m: The coffee plant is not a bean plant.

112524.q: What happens to green coffee beans when they are roasted?
a: They turn brown and develop their aroma
112524.e: Raw coffee is greenish and hardly tastes of coffee. Only the heat of roasting creates hundreds of aroma substances and the brown colour.
112524.m: Only roasting gives coffee beans their brown colour and aroma.

112525.q: What are black and green tea made from?
a: From the leaves of the tea bush
112525.e: Black and green tea come from the same tea bush, Camellia sinensis. It is related to camellias.
112525.m: Real tea comes from the leaves of the tea bush.

112526.q: What makes black tea different from green tea?
a: Black tea is oxidised, green tea is not
Black tea is made from roots
Green tea is made from fruits
112526.e: For black tea, the rolled leaves are left to react with oxygen, which makes them dark. Green tea is heated quickly so that this does not happen.
112526.m: Black and green tea come from the same bush but are processed differently.

112527.q: Which country produces the most tea in the world?
112527.e: China is the home of tea culture and today harvests by far the most tea. India comes second.
112527.m: China produces more tea than any other country.

112528.q: Which kind of tea is named after a town at the foot of the Himalayas in India?
112528.e: Darjeeling is a town in West Bengal, around which tea is grown at high altitudes. Assam, on the other hand, is an Indian state in the lowlands.
112528.m: Darjeeling tea grows on the slopes of the Himalayas.

112529.q: Under which name is tea from Sri Lanka still sold today?
112529.e: Until 1972 Sri Lanka was called Ceylon. The name has survived as a brand for the island's tea.
112529.m: Tea from Sri Lanka is still called Ceylon tea today.

112530.q: Which parts of the tea bush are harvested for tea?
112530.e: Mainly the shoot tips with the bud and the two youngest leaves are harvested. They make the finest tea.
112530.m: For tea, the young leaves and buds of the tea bush are picked.

112531.q: Strictly speaking, why is peppermint tea not “real” tea?
a: It does not come from the tea bush
112531.e: Only an infusion from the tea bush counts as real tea. Infusions of peppermint, camomile or fruit are called herbal or fruit teas.
112531.m: Only an infusion of tea bush leaves is real tea.

112532.q: What is the Japanese green tea called that is whisked with water as a fine powder?
112532.e: For matcha, shaded tea leaves are ground into a fine powder and whisked with a bamboo whisk. Sencha, on the other hand, is a leaf tea.
112532.m: Matcha is powdered green tea from Japan.

112533.q: Why are tea bushes on plantations cut back regularly?
a: So that they stay low and are easy to pick
So that they flower and fruit faster
So that they do not freeze in winter
So that they need less water
112533.e: In the wild, the tea bush can become a tree more than ten metres tall. On plantations it is kept about hip-high so that the pickers can reach the shoots.
112533.m: Tea bushes are kept low so that the leaves are easy to pick.

112534.q: In which climate zones is sugar cane mainly grown?
a: High in the mountains above 4,000 metres
112534.e: Sugar cane needs lots of warmth, sun and water and cannot stand frost. That is why it grows mainly in warm countries around the equator.
112534.m: Sugar cane grows in warm areas of the tropics and subtropics.

112535.q: In which part of the plant does sugar cane store its sugar?
112535.e: The sugar collects in the juice of the thick stalks. The stems are cut and pressed.
112535.m: In sugar cane, the sugar is in the juice of the stems.

112536.q: Which country harvests the most sugar cane in the world?
112536.e: Brazil produces around 40 per cent of the world's sugar cane, ahead of India. In the past the Caribbean was an important growing area.
112536.m: Brazil is the world's biggest sugar cane producer.

112537.q: Roughly how tall does sugar cane grow?
112537.e: Sugar cane stalks usually grow 3 to 6 metres tall and a few centimetres thick. This makes it one of the biggest grasses.
112537.m: Sugar cane grows several metres tall.

112538.q: Apart from sugar, what is sugar cane used for in large amounts in Brazil?
112538.e: The sugary juice is fermented into alcohol (ethanol), which is used as fuel in Brazil. Many cars there run on ethanol or petrol.
112538.m: In Brazil, many cars run on ethanol made from sugar cane.

112539.q: What is often done with the fibres left over after pressing sugar cane?
a: They are burnt to produce energy
They are thrown into the sea
112539.e: The crushed stalk fibres are often burnt in the sugar factories. This produces heat and electricity. They can also be made into paper and tableware.
112539.m: The leftovers of sugar cane provide energy.

112540.q: What is the dark, sticky syrup left over from making sugar called?
112540.e: Molasses still contains sugar that no longer crystallises, and many minerals. It is used as animal feed, for baking and for fermentation.
112540.m: Molasses is a dark syrup produced when making sugar.

112541.q: From which plant is sugar made in Switzerland?
112541.e: Sugar cane only grows in warm countries. In Switzerland sugar is made from sugar beet, for example in Aarberg and Frauenfeld.
112541.m: In Switzerland, sugar is made from sugar beet.

112542.q: Which region does the oil palm originally come from?
112542.e: The African oil palm (Elaeis guineensis) is native to western Africa. Today it is grown in many tropical countries.
112542.m: The oil palm originally comes from West Africa.

112543.q: Which two countries together produce most of the world's palm oil?
112543.e: Together, Indonesia and Malaysia supply well over three quarters of palm oil. Large areas of rainforest there were turned into plantations for this.
112543.m: Most palm oil comes from Indonesia and Malaysia.

112544.q: What colour is raw, untreated palm oil?
112544.e: The fruit flesh of the oil palm contains lots of natural colouring, so raw palm oil is a strong orange-red. When it is refined, it becomes pale and almost tasteless.

112545.q: What is the oil pressed from the seeds of the oil palm called?
112545.e: Each fruit has a hard stone with a seed inside. A second oil is made from it, used mainly for soap and cosmetics.
112545.m: Palm kernel oil is made from the kernels of the oil palm.

112546.q: Why does the food industry like using palm oil so much?
a: It is cheap and semi-solid at room temperature
It contains especially lots of protein
It contains especially lots of vitamin C
112546.e: Palm oil is cheap, keeps for a long time and is spreadable. That is why it is in margarine, baked goods, spreads and ready meals.
112546.m: Palm oil is cheap, keeps well and is spreadable, so it is in many foods.

112547.q: Roughly how many years does it take for a young oil palm to bear its first fruit?
112547.e: Oil palms bear their first fruit about three years after planting and give good harvests after five to six years. Plantations are used for around 25 years, until the palms are too tall to harvest.
112547.m: An oil palm bears fruit after just a few years.

112548.q: Which great ape is losing especially large amounts of habitat to palm oil plantations on Borneo and Sumatra?
112548.e: Orangutans live only in the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra. All three species of orangutan are considered threatened with extinction.
112548.m: The orangutan is especially threatened by palm oil plantations.

112549.q: Which statement about the oil yield of the oil palm is true?
a: It produces more oil per hectare than any other oil crop
It produces less oil per hectare than rapeseed
It only produces oil after a hundred years
It only produces oil every ten years
112549.e: An oil palm plantation produces several times as much oil per hectare as rapeseed, soya or sunflowers. Replacing it with other oils would therefore need more land.
112549.m: On the same area, the oil palm produces more oil than any other oil crop.

a: Rainforest is often cut down for plantations
It is the most expensive oil in the world
112550.e: In Indonesia and Malaysia, large areas of rainforest have been cleared for oil palms. That is why there are rules and labels for sustainable palm oil.
112550.m: Palm oil plantations often replace rainforest.

112551.q: Roughly how long is a single vanilla flower open?
112551.e: Each vanilla flower opens on just one single day. If it is not pollinated during this time, it wilts and forms no fruit.
112551.m: A vanilla flower is open for only about one day.

112552.q: Which country does vanilla originally come from?
112552.e: The Aztecs already flavoured their cocoa drink with vanilla. Spanish conquerors brought it to Europe in the 16th century.

112553.q: Which country produces the most vanilla today?
112553.e: The island of Madagascar in the Indian Ocean supplies most of the world's real vanilla. A cyclone there can make vanilla prices rise sharply all over the world.
112553.m: Most of the world's vanilla comes from Madagascar.

112554.q: What is the most important flavour substance in vanilla called?
112554.e: Vanillin only forms in the pod during fermentation. Today vanillin is also made artificially, because real vanilla is very expensive.
112554.m: The most important flavour substance in vanilla is called vanillin.

112555.q: What did a twelve-year-old boy invent for vanilla growing in 1841?
a: A simple way to pollinate the flowers by hand
A machine for harvesting the pods
A recipe for vanilla ice cream
112555.e: Edmond Albius was an enslaved boy on an island in the Indian Ocean. He pollinated the flowers by hand with a small stick. This method is still used today.
112555.m: Vanilla flowers are still pollinated by hand with a small stick today.

112556.q: Why does vanilla usually have to be pollinated by hand outside its homeland?
a: Its natural pollinators are missing there
112556.e: In vanilla's homeland, mainly certain bees pollinate the flowers. Elsewhere these animals do not exist, so every flower must be pollinated by hand.
112556.m: Outside its homeland, vanilla is pollinated by hand because suitable pollinators are missing.

112557.q: What are the tiny black dots in real vanilla ice cream?
112557.e: A vanilla fruit contains thousands of tiny black seeds. They are scraped out of the pod once it is cut open and added to ice cream or custard, for example.
112557.m: The black dots in vanilla ice cream are vanilla seeds.

a: Vanilla from islands in the Indian Ocean
Vanilla from the forests of France
112558.e: The island of Réunion used to be called Île Bourbon. Today real vanilla from this region, especially from Madagascar and Réunion, is called Bourbon vanilla.
112558.m: Bourbon vanilla comes from islands in the Indian Ocean.

112559.q: How does the vanilla plant grow?
112559.e: Vanilla grows as a vine and climbs up trees or support posts with its aerial roots. On plantations it is kept at a height you can reach.
112559.m: Vanilla climbs up trees as a vine.

112560.q: Which region does pepper originally come from?
112560.e: Pepper comes from the Malabar Coast in what is now the Indian state of Kerala. From there it was traded as far as Rome in ancient times.
112560.m: Pepper originally comes from the south-west of India.

112561.q: What do black, white and green pepper have in common?
a: They all come from the same plant
They come from three different trees
They are all made from roots
112561.e: All three are fruits of Piper nigrum. They only differ in when they are harvested and how they are processed.
112561.m: Black, white and green pepper all come from the same plant.

112562.e: The fruits are harvested while still green and dried in the sun. This makes their skin black and wrinkly.
112562.m: Black pepper is dried pepper fruit picked before it is ripe.

a: The fruit flesh is removed from ripe fruits
Black pepper is mixed with salt
112563.e: For white pepper, ripe fruits are soaked in water until the outer layer comes off. What is left is the pale seed.
112563.m: White pepper is the seed of ripe pepper fruit without the fruit flesh.

112564.e: Piperine is the hot substance in pepper. Capsaicin, on the other hand, is the hot substance in chillies.
112564.m: Pepper is hot because of the substance piperine.

112565.q: Which country produces the most pepper today (as of 2022)?
112565.e: Vietnam has greatly expanded pepper growing and supplies about a third of the world harvest. India, the home of pepper, is further behind.
112565.m: Vietnam is the world's biggest pepper producer today.

112566.q: Which sailor was the first European to reach India, the land of pepper, by sea in 1498?
112566.e: The Portuguese Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa and landed in Calicut on the Malabar Coast. After that Portugal could fetch pepper directly from India.
112566.m: Vasco da Gama found the sea route to India in 1498.

112567.q: Why is “pink pepper” not real pepper?
a: It comes from a completely different plant
112567.e: Pink berries come from the Peruvian or Brazilian pepper tree (genus Schinus). This is not related to real pepper.
112567.m: Pink pepper does not come from the pepper plant but from the pepper tree.

112568.q: What kind of plant is the cinnamon tree?
a: A dwarf shrub of the tundra
112568.e: The cinnamon tree grows in the tropics of Asia and has leathery leaves all year round. On plantations it is cut back again and again so that lots of young shoots grow.
112568.m: The cinnamon tree is an evergreen tree of the tropics.

112569.q: What are the two most important kinds of cinnamon called?
112569.e: Ceylon cinnamon is thought of as finer and milder; cassia cinnamon from China is stronger and cheaper. Supermarkets mostly sell cassia cinnamon.
112569.m: The most important kinds of cinnamon are Ceylon and cassia.

112570.q: Which part of the world does cinnamon originally come from?
112570.e: Cinnamon trees grow in the tropics of Asia, for example in Sri Lanka, India and China. From there the spice came to Europe.

112571.q: Why should you not eat cassia cinnamon in very large amounts?
a: It contains a lot of coumarin
It contains a lot of caffeine
It contains a lot of alcohol
It contains a lot of cyanide
112571.e: In large amounts, coumarin can damage the liver. Cassia cinnamon contains much more of it than Ceylon cinnamon, but normal amounts in baking are considered safe.
112571.m: Because of its coumarin, only eat cassia cinnamon in moderation.

a: The peeled bark rolls up as it dries
Cinnamon powder is pressed into sticks
The roots are cut into pieces
112572.e: The thin inner bark is peeled off and dried. As it dries, it rolls up into little tubes by itself.
112572.m: Cinnamon sticks are dried, rolled-up pieces of bark.

112573.q: What do people in Switzerland like to sprinkle on rice pudding?
112573.e: Cinnamon goes well with sweet dishes. It is very popular on rice pudding, in apple sauce or in Christmas biscuits.

112574.q: Which Swiss Christmas biscuits are baked from almonds, egg white, sugar and cinnamon and covered with white icing?
112574.e: Cinnamon stars are cut out of a dough made of ground almonds and glazed with beaten egg white. Mailänderli, on the other hand, are butter biscuits.
112574.m: Cinnamon stars are Christmas biscuits with almonds and cinnamon.

112575.q: Why was cinnamon very expensive in Europe in the past?
a: It came from Asia along long trade routes
Only kings were allowed to eat it
112575.e: Cinnamon was brought from Asia over long distances by ship and caravan. The long journey made it precious.
112575.m: Spices from Asia used to be very precious in Europe.

112576.q: Which mountain range does quinoa come from?
112576.e: Quinoa has been grown in the highlands of Peru and Bolivia for thousands of years. There it grows even at heights of around 4,000 metres.
112576.m: Quinoa comes from the Andes in South America.

a: It is not a grass but is used like a cereal
It is a grass but is never eaten
It is made artificially in a laboratory
112577.e: Real cereals such as wheat or rice are grasses. Quinoa is not a grass, but it produces similar grains that are cooked like cereals.
112577.m: Quinoa is a pseudocereal because it is not a grass but is used like a cereal.

112578.q: Which vegetable is quinoa related to?
112578.e: Like spinach, beetroot and amaranth, quinoa belongs to the same plant family. It is not related to cereals.

112579.q: Why must you wash quinoa thoroughly before cooking it?
a: The grains are coated with bitter saponins
The grains are full of desert sand
Otherwise the grains stick together in the pan
112579.e: Saponins are soapy, bitter substances on the husks of the grains. They protect the plant from birds and insects and are removed by washing.
112579.m: Quinoa is washed to remove the bitter saponins.

112580.q: Why is quinoa considered an especially valuable food?
a: It contains a lot of protein
It contains a lot of caffeine
It contains a lot of alcohol
It contains a lot of table salt
112580.e: Quinoa provides lots of protein, minerals and fibre. That is why the UN even declared 2013 the International Year of Quinoa.

112581.q: For which ancient people of the Andes was quinoa an important staple food?
112581.e: The Inca grew large amounts of quinoa alongside potatoes and maize. They saw it as a sacred plant.
112581.m: For the Inca, quinoa was a sacred staple food.

112582.q: Which property makes quinoa suitable for people with coeliac disease?
112582.e: People with coeliac disease cannot tolerate the protein gluten from wheat, rye and barley. Quinoa contains no gluten.
112582.m: Quinoa contains no gluten, so it is suitable for coeliac disease.

112583.q: Which two countries are the world's biggest quinoa producers?
112583.e: Almost the whole world harvest comes from Peru and Bolivia. But quinoa is now also grown in Europe, even in Switzerland.
112583.m: Most quinoa grows in Peru and Bolivia.

112584.q: Is the sweet potato closely related to the potato?
a: No, it belongs to a different plant family
Yes, it is a variety of potato
Yes, it is a sugared potato
Yes, both grow on the same bush
112584.e: The sweet potato belongs to the bindweed family. The potato belongs to the nightshade family. Despite the name, they are only distantly related.
112584.m: The sweet potato is not a real potato.

112585.q: Which other part of the sweet potato plant is eaten as a vegetable in many countries in Asia and Africa?
112585.e: The young leaves and shoot tips of the sweet potato are cooked in a similar way to spinach. They contain lots of vitamins and minerals.
112585.m: People also eat the young leaves of the sweet potato.

112586.q: Which region of the world does the sweet potato originally come from?
